verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You feel overlooked after being passed over for promotion again. Bhartrihari tells you that serving a master means being called dull if you stay quiet, or a show-off if you speak. This verse names the bind you face today: whatever you do, it gets twisted. Let the verse hold the shape of that impossible position.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks from the section on the wicked. He addresses anyone who serves a master. He lists the traps of serving a cruel boss. Stay quiet and you are called dull. Speak well and you are called a babbler. Stay close and you are called pushy. Keep away and you are called lacking confidence. Be patient and you are called weak. Refuse to tolerate abuse and you are called ill bred. Serving another in this way is a heavy duty. It lies beyond the reach even of those who practice yoga. You are caught in a bind where every move gets twisted into a fault. The verse names this impossible position without asking you to fix it today.

verse_text.speaker: Sutikshna
verse_text.setting: The young sage Sutikshna hears Ram is coming and runs to meet him, full of doubt about himself.
verse_text.line: I have no devotion, no wisdom, no steady love. But he loves the one who has nowhere else to go.
verse_text.translation: 'Will Ram, my master, with his brother, meet me as he would his own servant? There is no firm trust in my heart; no devotion, detachment or wisdom in my mind; no good company, no yoga, chanting or sacrifice, no steady love for his lotus feet. But the ocean of compassion has one habit: the one who has no other refuge is dear to him.'

reading: You feel uneasy because your manager keeps giving visible projects to others, and you wonder if you are simply not leadership material. Sutikshna says he has no wisdom, no steady love, and nowhere else to go. Today, that same lack of perfect qualifications is exactly what makes you dear, because the compassionate one loves the one who has no other refuge.
meaning: The young sage Sutikshna runs to meet Ram. He is full of doubt about himself. He thinks he has no devotion, no wisdom, and no steady love. He has no discipline and no good company. Yet he trusts that Ram loves the one who has nowhere else to go. The verse says that lack of perfect qualifications does not keep you away. The one who loves simply holds close the person with no other refuge. Your doubt about leadership material is heard. Sutikshna had no wisdom or steady love either, and he was still held close. Your lack of perfect qualifications is not a barrier to being valued.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse_text.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse_text.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.

reading: You feel like you are not good enough for any work. Krishna hears Arjuna tell him that his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, and his body trembles. Your body is showing the same signs of fear right now. Let that trembling be the truth you sit with today, without judging it.
meaning: Arjuna speaks these words to Krishna on the battlefield. He sees his own kin standing in the enemy ranks. His body reacts before his mind can catch up. His limbs fail him. His mouth goes dry. His body shakes and his hair stands on end. The verse shows that a person can collapse under pressure even when they are known for strength. It proposes that a breakdown is a valid starting point, not a failure. You are facing public blame at work and now doubt your own worth. Arjuna's collapse shows that fear can strike anyone, even those seen as capable.

verse_text.speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
verse_text.setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
verse_text.line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.
verse_text.translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.

reading: Since the breakup, your weekends feel empty and you see that your friends belonged to him. Sita, held captive, tells Ram: I have you, and yet I look like someone with no one at all. That ache of being surrounded by people yet truly alone speaks to your Saturdays now. You still have your own worth, even when the company around you feels borrowed.
meaning: Sita speaks these words to Rama in the Sundara. She sends them through Hanuman after months of captivity in Lanka. She tells Rama that she has him as her protector and husband, yet she still appears to the world as someone utterly alone. The verse names the gap between having a devoted partner and feeling abandoned by every other bond. You still carry your own worth even when the circle around you feels borrowed and your weekends open up without him.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: After your divorce, you moved to a new city where you do not know a single person. Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever sees him everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him, nor he to them. In this unfamiliar place, that presence can meet you in the empty room and in the street today, so you are not alone in the new city.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching him the practice of meditation and the nature of a settled mind. He tells him that a person who sees Krishna present in all things and sees all things contained within Krishna will never be separated from him, and Arjuna will never be lost to Krishna. In this new city where you know no one, that same unbroken connection can meet you in the empty room and on the street.

verse_text.speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
verse_text.setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
verse_text.line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.
verse_text.translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.

reading: You feel empty since your closest friend moved abroad and you barely talk now. Sita told Ram, 'I have you, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.' That gap between having someone and feeling alone speaks to you today. You can sit with Ram and name this exact ache without fixing it.
meaning: Sita speaks these words to Rama through Hanuman. She has been held captive in Lanka for months. She knows Rama is her protector and her own. Yet she tells him she looks like someone with no one at all. She asks him to show his great kindness. The verse holds the gap between real belonging and the feeling of being alone. Your friend is still part of your life even across the distance, yet the silence leaves you feeling hollow. Sita names that same split.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: Day after day, night after night, the same chain of tasks repeats. Bali, sitting by his window, feels mocked by this endless cycle. You have been firefighting so long that nothing remains in the tank, and this verse names that exact weariness without asking you to fix it. Let the thought of this mockery sit with you as you close the door tonight.
meaning: Bali speaks these words to himself. He is a king who has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day he sits by his window and watches the same days and nights pass. He feels that the endless chain of tasks mocks him. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it. You have been firefighting so long that nothing remains in the tank. The verse names that weariness without asking you to fix it right now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You carry a pressure that never drops and a fatigue that keeps you pinned to the bed even on weekends. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and do not last. You can bear this weight patiently as it moves through you, trusting that the weekend stillness and the workday pressure are also contacts that pass.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna collapses in grief on the battlefield. Arjuna has lost his kin and sees only ruin ahead. Krishna reminds him that the true self is never born and never dies. The contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings arrive and depart. They do not endure. Arjuna must learn to bear them with patience. Your work pressure and the fatigue that pins you to the bed on weekends are contacts that come and go. They do not define what you are.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You lie awake with your mind spinning about whether the launch will work. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and as hard to hold as the wind. Your thoughts tonight are like that wind, refusing to be caught. Rest against the truth that even the finest archer found his mind unyielding, and let your body meet the stillness of your bed.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He admits that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He finds it as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees that the mind is difficult to master, yet he points to steady practice and letting go as the way to train it. Your mind tonight is doing exactly what Arjuna named, and it is not a failure on your part.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

reading: You feel colleagues with MBAs stand above your experience. Krishna tells Arjuna to raise himself by his own self and not let himself sink, for the self alone is the friend of the self. Your years of experience are your own ground to stand on; let them lift you up rather than push you down.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between two armies, unsure and heavy. Krishna tells him that a person must lift themselves by their own effort. A person must not let themselves sink. The self alone can be a friend to the self. The self alone can also become an enemy. The choice belongs to the one who acts. Your experience is real ground. It can hold you up instead of weighing you down.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You lose your temper with your child over homework and then hate yourself after. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born; from attachment comes desire, and from desire comes anger. That evening buildup over homework can be seen as the mind dwelling on the struggle before the snap. Notice the homework moment itself as the place where the fire begins.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna what a person of steady mind looks like in speech, posture and walk. Krishna answers that such a person rests within, unshaken by sorrow and master of the senses. He then traces how the mind moves: when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire comes anger. Your anger over homework is not a sudden collapse. It begins earlier, in the mind dwelling on the struggle before the snap.

verse_text.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles – Third Series, LII, p. 525
verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.listener: Mrs. Blodgett ('Aunt Roxy'), his hostess in Los Angeles
verse_text.setting: Letter of 2 May 1900, in failing health, near the end of his second American tour.
verse_text.line: I just want a bit of peace badly — pray for me.
verse_text.translation: Well, dear good mother, may all blessings attend you and peace. I just want a bit of peace badly — pray for me. With love to Kate,

reading: You feel angry as the slamming and yelling repeat each week. Swami Vivekananda wrote, "I just want a bit of peace badly — pray for me." In your exhaustion from raising kids, this admission of weariness speaks plainly to the strain you carry. Let his longing for rest meet the noise of your home today.
meaning: Swami Vivekananda wrote this letter to Mrs Blodgett, his hostess in Los Angeles, on the second of May nineteen hundred. He was in failing health near the end of his second American tour. He told her that he wanted a bit of peace badly and asked her to pray for him. He signed it with love to Kate. His weariness mirrors the strain of your own home, where the weekly slamming and yelling leave little room to breathe.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You are furious because your lead dumped his work on you, and after snapping in standup you now feel like the problem. Bhartrihari writes that if you keep quiet you are dull, but if you speak up you are a babbler, and serving a boss is harder than yoga. In this moment, the verse simply names the trap you are caught in: any response you make gets twisted against you.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines as a warning to anyone who serves a cruel master. He lists the impossible choices a subordinate faces. Stay silent and you are called dull. Speak well and you are called a show-off. Stay close and you are pushy. Keep away and you lack confidence. Be patient and you are weak. Refuse to tolerate abuse and you are ill-bred. The verse proposes that serving a wicked boss is a trap where every move is twisted, and it is harder than yoga because there is no right answer. Your lead has trapped you in exactly this bind, and your anger at being made the problem is the trap speaking.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You are waiting on emergency leave while your dad is in hospice in Delhi. Krishna, far from home, tells his mother Yashoda that since he left her, no one has called him by his pet name. Like him, you may feel unseen in this distant place, yet your name and bond remain known beyond where you are right now.
meaning: Krishna sends a message from Mathura to his mother Yashoda, far from her home. He tells her that since the day he left her, no one has called him by his pet name Kanhaiya. Because of that, he has not eaten his morning breakfast or his evening warm milk. The verse shows that missing home is love. You are far from Delhi while your father is in hospice, and the waiting is heavy. The verse shows that being away does not erase the bond that names you.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You are watching your mother slowly pass away from late-stage cancer. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in his chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Like him, you too can set down the weight you are carrying and simply sit with what is happening right now, right beside her.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra from the battlefield. Arjuna stands between two armies and sees his own kin. He trembles. His bow slips from his hand. He sinks onto the chariot seat and will not fight. The verse records this collapse. It shows that a breakdown is not a failure. It is simply the place where the teaching begins.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You missed your mother's surgery because leave was denied, and her saying it is fine has not quieted the thought. Arjuna asks Krishna what drives a person to do wrong even against their will, as if pushed by force. This verse names that pull without judging your choice, leaving you with the image of being driven rather than freely failing.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong against their own will, as if pushed by some outside force. Krishna answers that it is desire which has not been met. That unmet want turns into anger and clouds a person's judgment. The verse says you can see this pull clearly and then master it. Your mother says she is fine, yet the thought of missing her surgery will not leave you. The verse names the force that moves you even when you do not want to move.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You spoke of saying in anger that you would send your father to an old age home, and now you cannot meet his eyes. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against his will, as if pushed by force. That moment of anger may feel like it came from outside you, yet the question remains open: the words are already out, but your father’s gaze is still here, and you can choose how to stand before it today.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even when they do not want to, as if pushed by force from outside. Krishna answers that it is desire which has not been met. That unmet desire turns into anger. Anger then clouds a person's wisdom. The verse proposes that you see this chain clearly. Once you see it, you can begin to master the desire instead of being mastered by it. The anger that made you speak those words came from a desire that was blocked. Seeing that link does not erase what you said, but it gives you a place to stand with your father now.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You yelled at your grandmother when she asked the same question for the fifth time, and she went quiet. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against his will, as if pushed by force. Your temper may feel like a force that moved before you could stop it, and that quietness afterward can sit heavily with you today.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against his own will, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this anger is the enemy that clouds a person's wisdom like smoke over a fire. He tells Arjuna to master this force rather than let it master him. Your temper may feel like a force that moved before you could stop it, and that quietness afterward can sit heavily with you today.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You spoke of anger arriving fast and guilt remaining after words you said in rage to your business partner. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against his will, as if pushed by force. That fast anger may have felt like an outside push, yet the guilt staying behind is yours to carry. Today, the partnership is gone, and the verse simply names the force you felt.
meaning: Arjuna, the warrior prince, asks Krishna, his charioteer and guide, why a person commits wrong actions even when they do not wish to, as though compelled by force. Krishna answers that it is desire which has not been met. When that desire is blocked, it turns into anger. This anger then clouds a person's wisdom and judgment, much like smoke veils a fire. The teaching is that this desire is the true enemy, and one must learn to master it rather than be mastered by it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: Even if you were the worst wrongdoer of all, the raft of wisdom would carry you across.
verse_text.translation: Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners, you will cross over all wrongdoing by the raft of knowledge alone.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that even if you were the worst wrongdoer of all, the raft of wisdom would carry you across. The guilt that stays with you after the anger speaks as if you are permanently what you did. The verse sees this guilt as an ocean you can cross, with the river still there behind you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: As a blazing fire turns wood to ash, real understanding burns away the hold of past actions.
verse_text.translation: As a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that as a blazing fire turns wood to ash, real understanding burns away the hold of past actions. Your anger flared and words were spoken, yet the guilt that lingers is what the fire of knowledge addresses. Let this understanding reduce the grip of what already happened, so you stand on the ash of the event itself.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse_text.line: Even if you've done great wrong, the moment you turn wholeheartedly, count yourself among the good.
verse_text.translation: Even if one of very bad conduct worships me with undivided devotion, he should be regarded as good, for he has resolved rightly.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that even if you have done great wrong, the moment you turn wholeheartedly you are counted among the good, because your resolve is right. Your anger flared fast and the partnership is gone, yet this turn toward what is right is itself the ground beneath your feet today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse_text.line: Such a person soon turns good and finds lasting peace. Mark it: no one devoted to me is ever lost.
verse_text.translation: He soon becomes righteous and attains lasting peace. Kaunteya, declare it boldly: my devotee never perishes.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that someone who turns wholeheartedly to devotion soon becomes righteous and finds lasting peace, and adds that no devotee of his is ever lost. The anger that flared and the guilt that stayed can shift as you choose your next step. You could write one sentence today describing what you will do differently in the next difficult conversation.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna's final counsel: act with devotion, reflect, choose, and take refuge.
verse_text.line: Lean on me alone. I will free you from every wrong. Don't worry.
verse_text.translation: Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone. I will free you from all sins; do not grieve.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to abandon all dharmas and take refuge in him alone, promising to free him from every wrong and telling him not to grieve. You could set down the partnership's weight for a few minutes today, letting the guilt stay without carrying it through the rest of your work.

story.title: Yudhishthira after the war
story.summary: Yudhishthira won the war and could not bear it. So many of his own family were dead, and he blamed himself. He wanted to give up the throne and go into the forest for good. One after another, his brothers, Draupadi, and the sages Devasthana and Vyasa argued with him about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life. Slowly he agreed to stay and rule, and to spend what was left of his life doing good.
story.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.

days.reading: Yudhishthira won the war yet wanted to disappear because so many of his own family were dead and he blamed himself. This mirrors the anger that came fast and the guilt that stayed after unforgivable things were said to your business partner. The story shows that guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end; the good you do next counts, so you can stay and rule what remains.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You mention that nothing seems worth the effort anymore and you have dropped out with no direction. Rama's attendant tells King Dasharatha that the prince no longer lights up at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work, but simply keeps silent. In your quiet now, the same withdrawal is present without judgment, and the silence itself can be where something new begins to gather.
meaning: Rama's attendant speaks to the worried King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Sixteen-year-old Rama has come home and quietly withdrawn. He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just keeps silent. The verse proposes that this loss of interest is not mere laziness or illness. It is the first stirring of deeper questions, provided someone helps the young prince through it. Your silence after dropping out carries the same withdrawal, and it can be where better questions begin to form.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You said that after so much effort, nothing came of it, and now nothing feels like it matters. Young Rama asks, 'What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?' His question points to a space where outcomes no longer define you, leaving room to simply sit with the question of who you are beyond what your hands have gained.
meaning: Young Rama has just returned from his travels. He sits in his father's court before the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha. He tells them that nothing interests him anymore. He asks what kingship or pleasure mean to him. He asks who he is and what all of this is for. He suggests that if the world is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks whose it really is and what anyone has gained. Your own effort has left you with empty hands, and now the weight of that loss makes everything feel pointless.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: Fifteen years of twelve-hour days built your business, and now the routine feels hollow. Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and says that day and night, the same tasks repeat, and a thinking person feels mocked by it. Your own rhythm of endless doing might mirror that same weariness today, leaving you tired in a way rest does not fix.
meaning: The demon king Bali has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day he sits by his window and sees that day follows night and the same tasks return without end. He speaks these words to himself. He means that a thinking person who notices this endless loop feels mocked by it. The verse proposes that the work itself is not the problem. The mind that runs the loop must be mastered through practice. Your fifteen years of long days built something real, yet the rhythm now leaves you hollow and tired in a way rest does not touch.

verse_text.speaker: Nidagha
verse_text.setting: Nidagha on craving.
verse_text.line: Every good quality I take up, craving gnaws through, like a mouse chewing a string.
verse_text.translation: Whatever good quality I take refuge in, great sage, craving cuts it away, as a mouse gnaws through a string.

reading: You plan to study after work, yet you end up scrolling until 1am. Nidagha says that whatever good quality he takes up, craving gnaws through it like a mouse chewing a string. That same gnawing may be at work when your intention to study meets the phone. Notice the string fraying tonight.
meaning: Nidagha speaks to his teacher Ribhu after returning from a pilgrimage feeling empty. He tells Ribhu that no matter what good quality he tries to hold onto, craving cuts it away like a mouse chewing through a string. He names the restless mind and admits that mastering it is harder than drinking the ocean. The same gnawing may be at work when your intention to study meets the phone.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You carry a firm resolve for your GATE preparation, yet the day slips away before you even begin. Savitri tells her father-in-law that she started this vow with determination, and that same determination carries it to the end. Let your own resolve anchor the start of each study day, so the hours you set aside actually become the hours you keep.
meaning: Savitri speaks to Dyumatsena, her father-in-law, after she learns that her husband Satyavan will die within three days. She has begun a hard three night vow. He is worried for her. She tells him not to be distressed. She says she will see the vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end. Your resolve for the GATE exam is real, but the morning still drifts away before the books open.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one the world follows. You want to keep your feet on the ground after your business’s best year ever. Let your groundedness be the standard your team and peers quietly follow.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is caught between duty and doubt. Krishna explains that even those who are fulfilled and have nothing left to gain still act. They work for the sake of the world. Others watch what they do. They copy the action, not the words. The standard a respected person sets becomes the path the world follows. Your best year ever brings real weight. The gratitude you feel can quietly shape how your team and peers show up next.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel that all is well and carry peace and gratitude in your heart. The poet asks what generous austerity brought this freedom to wander, food without humiliation, good company, and a mind that stirs only gently. Today, this view invites you to rest in the simple calm you already hold, without searching for any other reason.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his Worship of Shiva to the reader. He reflects on a life of quiet ease. He names the freedom to wander, food eaten without shame, the company of good people, and learning that brings only calm. He notes that his mind stays gentle even when it looks outward for long. He wonders what generous austerity earned him such a life. He offers gratitude for simplicity and devotion without rivalry between forms of God. You rest in the peace and gratitude you already carry. The verse simply holds up what you feel and asks what earned it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You feel drawn to Krishna in a way you didn't expect. Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him: the distressed, the curious, the needy, and the wise. Your unexpected pull counts as one of these welcome paths, and it can rest right there in your daily life with your kids.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands among two armies, unsure whether to fight. Krishna explains why most people miss the divine. He says four kinds of good people turn to the divine. They come in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome. Your unexpected pull toward Krishna is one of these welcome paths. It does not need a reason beyond itself to belong in your days with your children.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You have found calm through meditation and chanting, and now you want to go deeper toward God. Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship Him: those in distress, those curious, those in need, and the wise. Your peaceful path already counts as one of these welcomed ways, so your next step can simply be the deeper devotion you are already reaching for.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has asked why people miss the divine and who actually turns to it. Krishna answers that four kinds of good people worship. These are the distressed, the curious, those in need, and the wise. He makes clear that every reason for coming is accepted. Your calm from meditation and chanting already places you among those who turn toward the divine, and that welcome holds as you reach deeper.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You feel that the bliss while singing bhajans is what you want every moment. Krishna tells Arjuna that people come to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom, and all four kinds are good people. That same devotion you taste in song can be the anchor of your days now, a steady presence you return to whenever you sit.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He explains why most people miss the divine, caught in the play of qualities. He names four kinds of good people who turn to the divine. They come in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome. The devotion you taste in song is one of those four welcomes. It does not need to arrive through sorrow or search. It can simply be the wisdom that brings you back.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: Karmaṇy evādhikāras te: your right is to the action. Fear of failure is a fear about the fruit, which was never given to you to control. Krishna also closes the escape route: don't let this make you stop acting. Care, prepare and aim well, then put the outcome down.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield, just as Arjuna hesitates and asks what is right. Krishna tells him that a person has a right only to the action itself, never to its fruits. The teaching is to do the work fully and then let go of owning what comes after. It asks for complete effort without clinging to success or failure. Your right is to the work of launching the product. The money that follows is not yours to hold, so the fear of losing it cannot define your effort today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You are carrying the work of those who were cut, waiting to see if you are next. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact with the senses brings heat and cold, pleasure and pain, which come and go and do not last. You can bear this season of heavier load and uncertainty until it passes, just as the verse names cold and heat that move on.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. He has just laid down his weapons because he cannot bear to fight his own kin. Krishna begins to teach him about what endures. He tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These experiences come and go. They do not last. Arjuna must learn to bear them patiently. You are facing a season of heavier load and real uncertainty about your place. The verse names discomfort that moves on, and invites you to bear it without letting it define what remains.

verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: 'My Plan of Campaign', Madras, February 1897, on friends who turned critics.
verse_text.line: as soon as he dares to differ, that sympathy is gone, that love vanishes.
verse_text.translation: We hear so much tall talk in this world, of liberal ideas and sympathy with differences of opinion. That is very good, but as a fact, we find that one sympathises with another only so long as the other believes in everything he has to say, but as soon as he dares to differ, that sympathy is gone, that love vanishes.

reading: You carry the hurt of being pushed away for not meeting an expectation you could not control. Swami Vivekananda observed that sympathy vanishes the moment someone dares to differ. Today, that truth names the cold distance you face, and the silence that follows when love is withdrawn for simply being who you are.
meaning: Swami Vivekananda spoke these words to an audience at Victoria Hall in Madras during February of eighteen ninety seven. He was answering friends who had turned into critics of his work in America. He noted that people praise liberal ideas and sympathy for different opinions. Yet in practice they only support you while you agree with everything they say. The moment you dare to differ that sympathy disappears and the love vanishes. Your husband's family withdrew their care the moment your life did not match their expectation. That withdrawal was not about your worth.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
verse_text.translation: It is never born and never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

reading: You carry the hurt of missing your father’s cremation because you could not reach India in time. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. Let this truth sit beside your grief today, that the core of who your father was remains untouched even as you mourn the body you could not say goodbye to.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield, after Arjuna has laid down his weapons and confessed his despair over fighting his own kin. Krishna tells him that the self was never born and never dies. It does not come into being, and it will not cease to be. When the body is slain, the self is not slain. The body changes, but what is truly there endures beyond every loss. Your father is gone from this world, yet the core of who he was was never born and will never die. That truth can sit beside your grief without replacing it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: As we drop worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self leaves a worn body for a new one.
verse_text.translation: Just as a person casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that just as we set aside worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self leaves a worn body for a new one. This picture of the self moving on offers you ground to stand on, holding the reality of your loss without dismissing it. Let this image of setting aside what is worn rest with you today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Childhood, youth, old age: the body keeps changing. The wise aren't thrown by the next change.
verse_text.translation: Just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it passes on to another body. The steady person is not bewildered by this.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that just as the self passes through childhood, youth, and old age in one body, it passes on to another, and the steady person is not bewildered by this change. You carry the weight of missing your dad’s cremation across the distance. Today, let this truth give you ground to stand on: the body changes, and the wise are not thrown by the next change.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: No weapon cuts it, no fire burns it, no water wets it, no wind dries it.
verse_text.translation: Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, and wind does not dry it.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that no weapon cuts the self, no fire burns it, no water wets it, and no wind dries it. The loss your body suffered in India stays with the body alone and does not reach who your dad truly was. Let this be a solid place under your feet today.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha on the fourth gatekeeper: good company (satsanga).
verse_text.line: Even at your lowest and most helpless, don't let go of good company.
verse_text.translation: Even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little.

days.reading: Vasishtha tells Rama that even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little. In your grief over missing your father’s cremation, this points you toward steady companionship rather than isolation. Let one trusted friend sit with you today, or simply keep a line open to someone who listens.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse_text.line: A leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water: whatever is offered with love, I accept.
verse_text.translation: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, that offering of love from the pure-hearted I accept.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that he accepts a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or a little water when offered with love. You could place a single flower or a drop of water somewhere today as a small place for your love to rest. This gives your heart a concrete spot to hold what matters.

story.title: Bharata returns to Ayodhya
story.summary: Bharata was far away at his grandfather's home when his father, King Dasharatha, died. Messengers called him back without telling him why. He rode into an Ayodhya that had gone quiet, went looking for his father, and learned he was gone. He fell to the ground and wept. When he could stand again, the family priest Vasishtha gently told him it was time to perform the last rites, and he did them, grieving as he went.
story.lesson: Missing the goodbye is its own grief. Let yourself feel it, then do what love asks next.

days.reading: Valmiki’s Ramayana tells of Bharata returning to Ayodhya to find his father Dasharatha dead, then weeping and performing the last rites. Like you, he arrived too late for the cremation. Let that grief sit with you, then tend to what love asks next.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You are stretched across office deadlines, your son's exam prep, and a toddler. Krishna tells Arjuna that contacts of the senses bring heat and cold, pleasure and pain, which come and go and do not last. You can bear these passing touches until they move on.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield, after Arjuna has laid down his weapons and said he will not fight. The prince is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that the senses touching their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These come and go and do not last. He asks Arjuna to bear them patiently. The idea is that what a person truly is outlasts every loss and every passing pain.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You are facing work ramping up, daycare calling about a fever, and a partner travelling. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and do not last. This means the constant pressure you feel now is a contact that will move on. You can bear the daycare calls and the workload until they pass.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings come and go and do not last. He asks Arjuna to bear them patiently. What is real in a person outlasts every passing loss and pain. The pressure you feel now is a contact that will move on. You can bear the daycare calls and the workload until they pass.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You are starting your dream job on Monday, feeling excited and terrified you will mess it up. Lakshmana tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it; for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. This steadiness can meet you in that first week, turning your excitement into real reach as you step into the role.
meaning: Lakshman speaks to Ram at Lake Pampa. Sita has just been taken, and the beauty of the spring lake only deepens Ram's grief. Lakshman pulls him back by saying that enthusiasm is powerful. There is no strength greater than it. For the person who holds it, nothing in the world is out of reach. Your fear of messing up does not cancel the hope you carry. That hope is a real strength, and it can meet you in the first week of work.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You have been going back and forth on leaving your job for months, and it fills your day and night. Arjuna tells Krishna that his nature is overcome by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right, and he asks plainly to be taught what is best. Today, your own back-and-forth can be the honest ground where you stop forcing an answer and simply let a clearer voice speak into the choice before you.
meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield. His body trembles and his eyes fill with tears. He refuses to lift his bow. He tells Krishna that his nature is overcome by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right. He asks Krishna to tell him for certain what is best. He calls himself Krishna's student and says he has come to learn. Your own back-and-forth about the job is not a failure. It is the honest place where clarity can begin.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You described rushing from one thing to the next until the tiredness no longer leaves, even on holiday. Bhasa says the mind is carried along on endless waves of tasks, never getting a moment's rest, tangled in a net of reckonings. Today, your days may still hold that same chain, yet the verse points to the mind itself as the bird that faints under the weight. You might notice where your mind rests, even for a breath, between the next task.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to his old friend Vilasa, two men who grew up together in a forest hermitage and later spent lonely years in harsh austerities. When they meet again as old men, Vilasa admits he has never found peace. Bhasa tells him that years of hard effort without inner understanding leave a person exactly where they started. The mind is carried along on endless waves of tasks and never gets a moment's rest. It keeps tallying what has been done, what is being done, and what must still be done. Bhasa names the same spinning that has followed you from one duty to the next, even when the calendar says you are free.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You have a presentation tomorrow, and your mind keeps imagining people laughing and thinking you do not belong in this course. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and that holding it feels like holding the wind. Today, when those thoughts loop about tomorrow, you can notice them as that same restless wind rather than as proof of where you stand.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after hearing about steady discipline. He admits that his mind jumps around and will not stay put. He compares it to the wind, something you cannot catch in your hands. Krishna agrees that the mind is restless and hard to control. He adds that practice and letting go can slowly train it. Your mind is throwing up images of laughter and doubt right now. The verse names that exact restlessness and says it is hard for anyone.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You are caught between two costly paths, and neither feels clean. Arjuna tells Krishna that his nature is overcome by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right, so he asks plainly to be taught. In your own crossroads today, that same honesty—naming the weight without forcing a choice—can be the first step toward finding your way.
meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield. He has collapsed in tears and refuses to fight. He tells Krishna that his nature is overcome by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right. He asks Krishna to tell him plainly what is best. He says he is Krishna's student and has come to be taught. You face a choice where both paths cost someone something. Naming that you do not know which is right is not a failure. It is the honest ground from which a clearer path can begin.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You are caught between bringing your mother to you or returning to her, and the right path is not clear. Arjuna tells Krishna that his nature is overcome by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right, so he asks plainly to be taught. Today, your own uncertainty about Patna and this city can be spoken just as honestly, without forcing a choice between staying or leaving.
meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield. He has laid down his bow. His body shakes and his eyes fill with tears. He tells Krishna that his nature is stricken by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right. He asks Krishna to tell him plainly what is best. He calls himself a student and says he has come to learn. Your own confusion about Patna and this city can be named just as honestly, without forcing a choice between staying or leaving.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

reading: Hearing about your batchmate's promotion left you unable to congratulate him properly. Krishna tells Arjuna to raise himself by his own self and not let himself sink, for the self alone is the friend of the self. When comparison pushes you down, you can choose to lift yourself up instead of pushing yourself further down. Today, that means standing on your own side even when someone else moves ahead.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You keep buying things and upgrading phones and cars, yet nothing fills the emptiness. Young Rama asks, 'What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this?' His question points to the gap between chasing and meaning. You might sit with one upgraded object today and simply ask who you are beneath the upgrade.
meaning: Young Rama has returned from his travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha are there with him. Rama tells the sages that nothing holds his interest anymore. He asks what kingship means to him, what pleasures are, who he truly is, and what all this is for. He says that if the world is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks whose it really is and what anyone has gained. You are naming the same gap between the chase and the feeling of being alive.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You have applied to 200 jobs since your company shut down, and nothing has come of it. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Like Arjuna, you too can lay down the weight of the search and simply sit, letting the bow rest beside you in this in-between time.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just refused to fight his own kin. He drops his bow and arrows and sinks onto the chariot seat. His mind is overcome by grief. The verse shows that even a mighty warrior can freeze when the cost becomes too high. You are in the middle of a long search with no reply, and the stillness feels like failure.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You come home to an empty apartment, eat, sleep, repeat, with no one to share it with and no sure sense of what any of it is for. Rama's attendant tells King Dasharatha that the prince no longer lights up at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work, but simply keeps silent. That quiet withdrawal speaks to your days of going through the motions without connection or clear purpose.
meaning: Rama's attendant speaks to King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Sixteen-year-old Rama has stopped eating properly, stopped laughing, and sits alone in his rooms. The attendant reports that Rama no longer lights up at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work, but simply keeps silent. The verse proposes that this loss of interest is not mere illness or weakness, but the first stirring of real questions about life. Your own quiet withdrawal from the daily routine echoes Rama's. It is not a flaw in you, but the start of a deeper question about what matters.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Your temper spikes when your partner breaks an agreement, and later you lie awake replaying how loud you got. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. That same restlessness can show up tonight in the loops replaying your raised voice, without asking you to fix it.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after hearing about the discipline of meditation. He admits that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse proposes that the mind is difficult to control, yet steady practice and the act of letting go can gradually train it. That same restlessness can show up tonight in the loops replaying your raised voice, without asking you to fix it.

Then attachment becomes wanting. When wanting meets a block, it turns into anger. The verse proposes that steadiness means guarding where attention rests, because anger does not arrive from outside. It grows from what the mind has already been feeding. You grip the steering wheel so hard in traffic because your mind has been dwelling on what slows you down. It is the last link in a chain that starts with dwelling. That flash of rage at the changed brief is the final spark of a fire that began earlier, when you started dwelling on the new demand. The steadiness Krishna speaks of starts with noticing that shift.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You said your anger takes over in the moment and left things awkward with your best friend. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against his will, as if pushed by force. Your outburst may feel like it came from outside yourself, yet the verse simply names that struggle without judging the words you spoke.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even when he does not want to, as if pushed by some outside force. Krishna answers that desire which is blocked turns into anger. This anger is the enemy that clouds a person's wisdom, much as smoke hides fire. The verse proposes that a person can master this force only by seeing it clearly for what it is. Your outburst with your best friend may feel like it came from outside yourself, yet the verse simply names that struggle without judging the words you spoke.

Your flare at work begins earlier than the shout. The anger starts in the mind before anyone sees it.
