verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You feel stuck while others raise funding and you still work alone from your spare room. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Like him, you may simply be sitting down because the weight is too much right now. Your bow is not gone; it is resting in your hands.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid out his fear and his grief. He sees his kin standing ready to die. The weight of it crushes him. He lets his bow and arrows fall. He sinks down on the chariot seat. He cannot move. The verse shows a collapse. The strongest person can simply stop. You are watching others move ahead while you stay in your spare room. That gap can feel like a collapse. The verse names what happens when the weight becomes too much to carry alone.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You feel the sting each time you see updates from your former juniors who are now CXOs. Bhartrihari cries out to hope, saying he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart, asking how much longer hope will make him dance. Today, your pain might echo that same hollow performance, watching their success while your own worth feels buried.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines to his own hope from the section on the censure of craving. He has spent years digging for treasure and flattering kings to win favor. He admits he endured the taunts of the wicked, held back his tears, and laughed with an empty heart. He even folded his hands before those numbed by money. He asks hope how much longer it will make him dance in this futile way. Your pain echoes that same hollow performance, watching their success while your own worth feels buried.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: Seeing your peers move ahead while you apply from your parents' place weighs heavily on you. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in his chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Like him, you can set down the weight of comparison today and simply sit with where you are, right at this table.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra from the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid down his weapons and collapsed in his chariot. He is frozen by grief and refuses to fight his own kin. The verse records this collapse. It shows that even a mighty warrior can stop completely when sorrow takes over. You are not failing because you have paused while others move ahead.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

reading: You feel behind the other mums at school pickup. Krishna tells Arjuna to lift himself up by his own self and not let himself sink, because the self alone is the friend of the self. You can stand on your own side today, steady in the honour and insult of those school gates, raising yourself up rather than pushing down.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands in doubt, and Krishna tells him to be his own friend. The self alone can lift the self up, or let the self sink. A person is either their own best friend or their own worst enemy, and the choice belongs to them. You gave up your career and home to raise your children, and now the school gates feel like a place of falling behind. The verse says your own self can still lift you up, without needing to match the others.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You carry the weight of being the other one at every family dinner. Krishna tells Narada that harsh words from relatives keep burning him day after day. You might find that the comparison to your sister still stings in the room where everyone gathers. Let that fire-stick image remind you that the burn is real, and you are allowed to feel it without forcing the ache away.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing weary of feuds inside his own clan. He admits that the harsh words his relatives speak keep burning him repeatedly. He compares his heart to a fire-stick being churned by someone who wants flame. The verse proposes that in family conflict the only effective weapon is softness, patience and respect rather than force. You sit through dinners where your sister's success is the only story told. Krishna felt the same sting from his own kin, and the burn does not fade simply because the meal ends.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has lain on the shore for three days asking the ocean for a way across. No answer comes.
verse_text.line: Calm, patience, honesty and kind words: people who don't value them will read them as weakness.
verse_text.translation: See the ocean's arrogance: he does not even show himself. Calm, forbearance, straightforwardness and gentle speech, these virtues of the good, are taken by the unworthy as signs of weakness.

days.reading: Ram tells Lakshman that calm, patience, honesty and kind words are read as weakness by those who do not value them, pointing to the ocean's arrogance after three days of silence. Your hurt fits this view: the verse sees the slight coming from the other's failure to value gentleness, not from any flaw in you. Today, notice one moment at a family dinner where you stay calm, and let that steadiness be your own, not a sign for them to dismiss.

verse_text.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse_text.speaker: Prahlada (quoted by Draupadi)
verse_text.setting: Draupadi quotes old Prahlada answering his grandson: is forgiveness better, or force?
verse_text.line: Force isn't always right, and forgiveness isn't always right. Wisdom is knowing which the moment needs.
verse_text.translation: Force is not always best, and forgiveness is not always best. Know this for certain, my child: both have their place.

days.reading: Draupadi tells Yudhishthira that force is not always best, and forgiveness is not always best; both have their place. Since family words still sting, you do not have to choose forgiveness today. Stand on the truth that wisdom means waiting for the right moment, not rushing a decision.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Uttanka, furious that the war happened, threatens to curse Krishna for not stopping it.
verse_text.line: I tried hard to make peace. When people refuse to be reconciled, you can't force it.
verse_text.translation: I made every effort earlier to bring the Kauravas to peace. But they could not be brought to agree, however I tried.

days.reading: Krishna tells the angry sage Uttanka that he tried hard to bring peace, but when people refuse to be reconciled, you cannot force it. Your hurt from those family dinners is real, yet peace was never yours alone to make. You can stand on the ground that the door to harmony was closed by the other, not by you.

verse_text.speaker: Seer
verse_text.setting: The creation story: last of all, dharma is made.
verse_text.line: Nothing is higher than what is right. With it the weak can face the strong. What is right is truth.
verse_text.translation: Still he did not flourish. So he created a higher form, dharma. Dharma is the power over power; nothing is higher than dharma. Through dharma even a weak man can stand up to a strong one, as with the help of a king. That dharma is truth. So people say of one who speaks truth, 'He speaks dharma,' and of one who speaks dharma, 'He speaks truth.' Both are the same.

days.reading: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says that nothing is higher than what is right, and through it the weak can face the strong. You could let this be your footing today when family comparisons sting. Stand on what is right, letting truth carry you through.

verse_text.speaker: Kabandha
verse_text.setting: Ram is lost and grieving; Kabandha tells him to seek Sugriva, who has also lost his wife and home.
verse_text.line: Find a friend who knows your kind of trouble. You won't get through this alone.
verse_text.translation: You must make him your friend, best of friends. Thinking it over, I see no success for you without it.

days.reading: Kabandha tells the grieving Ram to find Sugriva, who has likewise lost his wife and home, and make him a sworn friend, because you will not get through this alone. You could reach out to one classmate who understands what it feels like to come second at family gatherings. That connection offers a steady presence beside you today.

story.title: Hanuman finds a friend in Lanka
story.summary: Searching Lanka, Hanuman is surprised to find a house with Ram's name on it. Its owner, Vibhishan, Ravana's brother, says he lives in Lanka like a tongue among teeth. Hanuman tells him even a restless monkey like himself was given Ram's love.
story.lesson: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.

days.reading: Hanuman finds Ravana’s brother Vibhishan living inside Lanka like a tongue among teeth, unable to share his values with those around him. Vibhishan admits he has no practice or love for Ram’s feet, yet trusts that grace alone brings a saint to meet him. You too live among people whose values do not match yours, and this scene shows how one true friendship in a hostile place can bring rest beyond words.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

reading: Your brother's shop runs twice as well, and relatives count it at every wedding. Krishna tells Arjuna to lift himself by his own self and not let himself sink, because the self alone is the friend of the self. You can stand on your own side today, steady in your own work, without measuring it against his.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between two armies, uncertain and afraid. Krishna tells him that a person must lift themselves by their own effort. They must not let themselves sink into despair. The self alone can be the friend of the self, or the self alone can be the enemy of the self. The choice belongs to the one who acts. Your brother's shop and the relatives at weddings do not decide the worth of your own work. You can choose to stand with yourself today.

Krishna tells Arjuna to lift himself by his own self and not let himself sink, for the self alone is the friend of the self. Your own steady presence can be the ground that holds you up today, rather than the pull of their comfort.

They must not allow themselves to sink. The self alone can be a friend, and the self alone can be an enemy. The choice belongs to the one who acts. You moved for a better life and now the comparison weighs on you. Your own steady presence can hold you up, instead of the pull of their comfort.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.

reading: Comparison is mostly a voice that pushes you down. Krishna says you can be your own friend or your own enemy, and asks you to lift yourself up. Start by noticing which one you've been lately.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is weighed down by doubt and grief. Krishna tells him that a person must raise themselves by their own effort. They must not let themselves sink. The self is both the friend and the enemy of the self. The choice between those two roles belongs entirely to the person. The comparison you feel is one side of that inner voice. It is the part that pushes you down instead of lifting you up.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse_text.line: Better your own path done imperfectly than someone else's done perfectly. Borrowed lives are dangerous.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, even done imperfectly, than the duty of another well done. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is full of fear.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that doing your own duty imperfectly is better than performing another's perfectly, because borrowed lives are dangerous. When you measure yourself against others, you quietly swap your own path for theirs and then grade yourself by their standard. Today, notice the pull to adopt someone else's rhythm, and return your attention to the task already in your hands.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how the wise live and work.
verse_text.line: Content with what comes, beyond envy, steady in success and failure, you stay free even while working.
verse_text.translation: Content with whatever comes unasked, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, the same in success and failure, even when acting he is not bound.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the wise stay content with whatever comes unasked, beyond envy, steady in success and failure, and remain free even while working. You do not have to chase every milestone others reach. Let your own effort be enough today, and notice one task you finish without measuring it against anyone else.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Drop the cravings, the sense of 'mine' and the 'I' that keeps score. That's where peace is.
verse_text.translation: The person who gives up all desires and moves about free from longing, without the sense of 'mine' and without ego, attains peace.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to drop the cravings, the sense of 'mine', and the 'I' that keeps score, because that is where peace is found. The voice comparing you to batchmates and cousins runs on that scorekeeper. Today, you can step off that tally and simply move through your working hours without keeping count.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.

story.title: The mongoose and the handful of flour
story.summary: At the end of Yudhishthira's grand horse sacrifice, a mongoose appeared with one side of its body made of gold. It declared that the whole sacrifice was worth less than a handful of flour. Once, it said, during a famine, a poor gleaner and his family each gave their last share of flour to a hungry guest. When the mongoose rolled in the flour that had spilled, half its body turned gold. It had gone to many great sacrifices since, hoping to turn the other half, and none had done it.
story.lesson: A small gift, honestly earned and given from little, outweighs the grandest show.

days.reading: The Mahabharata tells of a mongoose with half its body turned gold because it rolled in a poor family’s last handful of flour given to a hungry guest. That small, honest gift outweighed Yudhishthira’s grand sacrifice. Your peace is not measured by how much others have gained, but by the sincerity of what you offer from where you stand.

verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You japa every evening and want to lose yourself in His name. Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him—the distressed, the curious, the needy, and the wise—and all are welcome. Your evening practice already places you among those who turn to the divine, so rest in that name as the living thread of your days.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He is explaining why most people miss the divine and who instead turns toward it. He says four kinds of good people worship him. These are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He makes clear that any of these motives leads to the same path. Your evening japa already places you among those who turn toward the divine, whatever your reason may be.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. In your mock interviews this week, the questions are yours to answer, but the final round's result is not yours to hold. Let that keep your hands moving on Thursday without letting the outcome freeze you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the field before battle. Arjuna is afraid to fight because he cannot bear the cost of winning or losing. Krishna tells him to claim only the work itself. The outcome belongs to a larger order, not to Arjuna alone. The teaching is to act with full attention and then release any claim to the result. Your mock interviews belong to you. The final round result does not belong to you alone.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You face a big investor pitch next Tuesday and rehearse every night, yet still feel you will freeze in front of them. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, and that holding it feels like holding the wind. Your nightly rehearsals echo that same wind, and the pitch itself is the stage where it blows. Rest in the fact that the wind is real, not a failure of yours.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the field of battle. He admits that his mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna answers that practice and letting go can train the mind. Your nightly rehearsals sit inside that same wind. The pitch is simply the place where it blows.

verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna calls these mātrā-sparśa: contacts, things that touch you and move on. A deadline, a bad week, a hard meeting. They hurt while they last, they pass, and Krishna asks you to bear them (titikṣasva) until they do.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: Sitting on the floor watching your son take his first steps brought you to tears of thankfulness. The poet asks what generous austerity earned this freedom to wander at will, simple food, good company, and a mind that stirs only gently. You can hold that quiet moment on the floor as the calm this learning already brings.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
verse_text.translation: It is never born and never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

reading: You still make your amma's dal and cry into the pot. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is. Today, the love that shaped her dal remains beside your grief in that kitchen, unchanged even as your tears fall.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is bowed with grief over the elders and kin he must fight. Krishna tells him that the self inside every person was never born and never dies. It does not end when the body ends. The body is only a garment that changes. The self remains unborn, eternal, constant and ancient. It is not slain when the body is slain. The love that shaped your amma's dal was never born and will never die. It stays beside your grief even as you cry into the pot.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You took money from your parents' savings for your startup and lost it all, and their silence makes it heavier. This verse names that struggle without judging your choice, pointing to the force behind actions rather than the person alone. meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even when they do not want to, as if pushed by some force against their will. The verse proposes that a person can master this force only by seeing it clearly for what it is. Your guilt carries the weight of a force you did not fully name at the time. The text sees that force, not only the choice, and leaves room for you to look at it without adding more blame.

verse_text.speaker: Sutikshna
verse_text.setting: The young sage Sutikshna hears Ram is coming and runs to meet him, full of doubt about himself.
verse_text.line: I have no devotion, no wisdom, no steady love. But he loves the one who has nowhere else to go.
verse_text.translation: 'Will Ram, my master, with his brother, meet me as he would his own servant? There is no firm trust in my heart; no devotion, detachment or wisdom in my mind; no good company, no yoga, chanting or sacrifice, no steady love for his lotus feet. But the ocean of compassion has one habit: the one who has no other refuge is dear to him.'

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.

verse_text.translation: As a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.

verse_text.setting: Krishna's final counsel: act with devotion, reflect, choose, and take refuge.
verse_text.line: Lean on me alone. I will free you from every wrong. Don't worry.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna, 'Abandon all dharmas and take refuge in me alone. I will free you from all sins; do not grieve.' story.title: Yudhishthira after the war
story.summary: Yudhishthira won the war and could not bear it. So many of his own family were dead, and he blamed himself. He wanted to give up the throne and go into the forest for good. One after another, his brothers, Draupadi, and the sages Devasthana and Vyasa argued with him about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life. Slowly he agreed to stay and rule, and to spend what was left of his life doing good.
story.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.

days.reading: After winning the war, Yudhishthira could not bear the cost and wanted to disappear into the forest, weighed down by the deaths of his kin. Your guilt carries a similar weight, yet the story shows that staying to do good now matters more than the past you cannot undo. Let the next right action you take be your anchor today.

Krishna answers that desire, when blocked or unmet, turns into anger. That anger clouds a person's judgment and wisdom just as smoke hides a fire. The verse proposes that you see this chain clearly. Once you recognize desire turning into anger, you can begin to master it instead of being driven by it.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You have noticed weeks of steady calm where traffic and deadlines no longer get under your skin. The poet asks what generous austerity earned this freedom to wander at will, simple food without humiliation, good company, and learning whose only fruit is calm. Let this gentle, outward-looking mind remind you of the quiet mornings you wish to keep.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from a place of worship of Shiva. He looks at a life of quiet ease and wonders aloud. He names freedom to move as one wishes, food taken without shame, noble company, and learning that brings only calm. He asks what generous austerity earned these gifts. He offers gratitude for simplicity and devotion without rivalry between forms of God. You have found a steadiness that once felt out of reach, and the verse invites you to see it as a gift worth noticing.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: Krishna describes someone whose happiness, pleasure and light are all inside: antaḥ-sukhaḥ, antar-ārāmaḥ, antar-jyotiḥ. Good days still come from outside. This joy doesn't depend on them.

verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel a lightness in your chest these days and want to learn how to make it stay. Bhartrihari asks what generous austerity brought this freedom to wander at will, food without humiliation, good company, and learning whose only fruit is calm. You can rest in that gentle mind today, letting it stir only softly even as you look outward, and notice how this lightness already lives in your chest.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his Worship of Shiva. He is looking back at his own life. He has food that does not humiliate him. He wanders where he wants. He lives among good people. He learns things that bring calm. His mind barely stirs even when he looks at the world. He asks what generous austerity earned him all this. You carry a lightness in your chest right now. Bhartrihari asks what earned you this freedom and calm.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You mentioned a joy within and a wish to know it more deeply. Krishna tells Arjuna that one whose happiness, delight and light are all inside becomes one with Brahman and reaches lasting freedom. This inner glow you feel can keep growing as you explore it, without waiting for anything outside to change.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the yoga of knowledge. He describes the wise person who looks on all beings with an equal eye. Such a person is not lifted up by pleasure or brought down by pain. Their happiness lives inside them. Their delight lives inside them. Their light lives inside them. This yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman. The stillness you feel now has its own source. It does not depend on what comes next.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna sorts knowledge, action, doers, judgement, resolve and happiness by the three qualities.
verse_text.line: Some pleasure tastes like nectar at first and poison in the end. Know which kind you're choosing.
verse_text.translation: The happiness that comes from contact of the senses with their objects, like nectar at first and like poison in the end, is called rajasic.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that pleasure born from the senses meeting their objects tastes like nectar at first, yet like poison in the end; he names this rajasic happiness. Since you feel a peaceful delight within and wish to know it more deeply, this verse points to the difference between that inner steadiness and the fleeting pull of outer stimulation. Notice, in your daily rhythm, where a craving for stimulation begins, and let the nectar-then-poison pattern show you which source you are touching.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Unhooked from outside pleasures, you find a joy within that doesn't run out.
verse_text.translation: One whose self is unattached to outer contacts finds the happiness that is in the self. Joined to Brahman by yoga, he enjoys undying happiness.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that one unattached to outer contacts finds a happiness within that does not run out. This inner joy grows the more your delight rests on yourself alone. You already feel a quiet delight inside, so let that steady ground hold you today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: When the mind clears, sorrows start to dissolve, and understanding settles quickly.
verse_text.translation: In that clarity all sorrows come to an end; for one whose mind is clear, understanding soon becomes steady.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that when the mind clears, sorrows begin to dissolve and understanding settles quickly. This speaks to your peaceful state, where an inner delight already rests. Ground yourself today in that clear mind, letting understanding settle like still space.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna sorts knowledge, action, doers, judgement, resolve and happiness by the three qualities.
verse_text.line: Some joy tastes like poison at first and like nectar in the end. That joy is worth it.
verse_text.translation: That which is like poison at first and like nectar in the end, born from the clarity of one's own understanding, is called sattvic happiness.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that some joy tastes like poison at first and like nectar in the end, born from the clarity of your own understanding. Since a peaceful calm already lives within you, you could gently sit with one small practice today that feels difficult at the start, letting its deeper sweetness unfold.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on three kinds of food, effort, speech and giving.
verse_text.line: A calm mind, gentleness, quiet, self-restraint and a clean heart: that is discipline of mind.
verse_text.translation: Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint and purity of feeling: this is called austerity of the mind.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that a calm mind, gentleness, quiet, self-restraint and a clean heart make up the discipline of mind. Since a quiet joy already lives within you, you could let your speech rest for a few minutes today and notice that inner stillness without seeking anything new.

story.title: Bhushunda
story.summary: The sage Vasishtha travelled to a wish-fulfilling tree on Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who had watched whole ages of the world come and go and was still happy. Asked his secret, Bhushunda listed his habits. He didn't brood on the past or the future. He didn't fret about what he'd get next. Learning never made him proud. And he was glad when others were glad, and sad when they were sad.
story.lesson: A long, glad life comes from staying present, wanting little and staying kind.

days.reading: Bhushunda tells Vasishtha he stayed happy across endless ages because he did not brood on the past or fret about the future. This speaks to your peaceful inner state, showing that lasting joy grows when attention rests fully here. You can keep knowing that delight by letting go of what comes next.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You are in a gap year at home with your grandparents and have never felt this calm. Bhartrihari asks what generous austerity earned him this freedom to wander, simple food, noble company, and learning whose only fruit is calm. You can carry this gentle mind back into real life by noticing the quiet calm you already hold, not by chasing it elsewhere.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines as a reader addresses himself, reflecting on a life of quiet ease. He lists freedom to move as he wishes, food taken without shame, the company of noble people, and learning that yields only calm. He wonders what past discipline or austerity earned him this gentle state of mind, which remains undisturbed even when he looks outward for long. You are tasting this calm now in your grandparents' home, and the verse simply asks what earned it, so you can see it as something already yours.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You noticed that lately even bad days feel okay inside, whereas before you needed things to go well to feel happy. Krishna tells Arjuna that the one who is happy within, at ease within, and lit from within finds lasting freedom. This inner steadiness can meet you today exactly as you sit with work, letting you rest in the calm you are already sensing.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching the yoga of knowledge. He describes the wise person who looks on all beings with an equal eye. Such a person is not elated by good fortune or crushed by bad. They find their delight inside themselves. They see that sense pleasures begin and end, and they know these end in sorrow. Because they see clearly, they withstand desire and anger. The verse proposes that lasting freedom belongs to the one whose happiness, delight and light are all within. Your shift from needing good days to feeling okay inside bad ones is the first sign of that inner light.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You feel lighter inside lately, finding peace in what simply is, and want that to last. Krishna tells Arjuna that one who is happy within, at ease within, and lit from within finds lasting freedom. This points to a steadiness that stays even when outer days shift, resting in the same quiet you already know.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching the path of knowledge. Arjuna has asked about the nature of the wise person. Krishna describes someone who keeps happiness, delight and light inside themselves. This person does not depend on things that come and go. They become one with the highest reality and reach its peace. You already feel that inner lightness. This points to a steadiness that stays even when outer days shift, resting in the same quiet you already know.

reading: You find peace in the morning silence before the house wakes up. The poet Bhartrihari asks what generous austerity brought this freedom to wander at will, simple food, good company, and learning whose only fruit is calm. That stillness you cherish can be a quiet anchor through your day of caring, a gentle presence you return to whenever the hours grow loud.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks from a life of deliberate withdrawal near the Ganga. He addresses anyone who reads these lines. He lists four gifts. He can move where he wishes. He eats without bowing to another. He lives among worthy people. He studies in a way that only brings calm. His mind stays gentle even when it looks at the world. He wonders what quiet discipline earned him such a life. You already know the value of that early silence. The verse invites you to see it as a gift earned by quiet living, not by chance.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel a deep contentment and want it to last. Bhartrihari asks what generous austerity earned this freedom to wander at will, simple food without humiliation, noble company, and learning whose only fruit is calm. Your quiet mornings and steady work already hold this calm; let this gratitude rest simply on the life you have built.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines as a reflection on a life stripped of struggle. He sits with the quiet gifts of movement without chains, meals taken with dignity, the shelter of good people, and study that settles the mind rather than agitates it. He wonders aloud what past discipline or sacrifice could have earned such a gentle existence. The verse proposes that a simple life, free from rivalry and noise, is itself a rare fruit worth recognizing with gratitude.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You feel genuinely happy from your morning runs and journaling, yet you worry this joy is temporary. Krishna tells Arjuna that one whose happiness, delight and light are within becomes free and at ease. Your runs and pages can be part of that inner light, not just a passing mood.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching the yoga of knowledge. Arjuna has asked about the nature of the wise person. Krishna describes someone who treats all beings with an equal eye. Such a person is neither overjoyed nor broken. They find their delight inside themselves. They see that sense pleasures begin and then fade into sorrow. Because they see this clearly, they can stand firm against desire and anger. Their happiness does not come from outside things. Your runs and pages are feeding something inside you that does not depend on a good grade or a like. That is the start of a steadier joy.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: At seventy, you find joy in simple days and want to understand this happiness more deeply. The poet asks what generous austerity earned this freedom to wander at will, food without humiliation, good company, and a mind that stirs only gently. Today, your gratitude can rest in the quiet morning itself, noticing the calm that needs no deeper reason.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from his Worship of Shiva. He looks back on a life of quiet devotion by the Ganga. He lists freedom to wander, plain food without shame, noble company, learning that brings calm, and a mind that stays gentle. He asks what generous austerity earned him this. He offers gratitude for a simple life and devotion without rivalry between forms of God.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You find a deep calm when your baby finally sleeps, and you wish that same stillness could stay with you all day. Krishna tells Arjuna that the truly happy person is at ease within, lit from within. That inner light can keep you steady through the busy hours with your child, not just in the quiet moments after they rest.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching the yoga of knowledge. Arjuna has been listening to the nature of the wise. Krishna describes the person who sees clearly. This person keeps an even gaze toward all beings. They do not rise on joy or fall on grief. They find their delight inside themselves. They know that pleasures born from the senses end in sorrow. Because they see this, they withstand desire and anger. Their happiness does not come from outside things. It comes from within. The calm you feel when your baby sleeps comes from inside you. It is not the sleep itself that gives it, but your own stillness.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: Eating alone in the dining hall while others sit in tight groups is a heavy weight. Krishna tells Arjuna, See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. When you look around the room today, you might notice one shared thread in every face, a presence that stays close even when no one sits beside you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching him about meditation and a settled mind. He tells him that if a person sees him in everything and sees everything in him, then Krishna is never lost to that person, and that person is never lost to Krishna. You are far from home and eating alone while others sit in groups. This idea says your connection is not broken just because you are sitting by yourself.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You stay at home while your husband works long hours, and some days pass without another adult voice. Krishna tells Arjuna, See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. In the quiet of your home, this means the presence you seek is not limited by distance or silence; it is already woven into the very air around you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He is teaching him how to steady the mind through meditation. He tells Arjuna that a person who sees the divine presence in all things and sees all things within that presence will never be separated from it. The idea is that this mutual seeing creates a bond that distance or wandering thoughts cannot break. The presence you miss is not locked outside your door. It can meet you in the stillness of the rooms you share with your children.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna tells Arjuna where the divine is found.
verse_text.line: The divine lives in the heart of every being, yours included.
verse_text.translation: The Lord dwells in the heart of every being, Arjuna, moving all beings by his power as if mounted on a machine.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the Lord dwells in the heart of every being, moving them all. That presence is in your heart too, right here in this flat and this city, not only back home or in a temple. When a day passes without another adult’s voice, you can stand on the fact that you are not alone in your own chest.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna tells Arjuna who he is to every being.
verse_text.line: I am your goal, your support, your witness, your home, your shelter and your friend.
verse_text.translation: I am the goal, the sustainer, the master, the witness, the home, the refuge and the friend; the origin and the dissolution, the ground, the treasure-house and the undying seed.

days.reading: In one verse Krishna lists what he is to every being: goal, support, witness, home (nivāsaḥ), shelter (śaraṇam) and friend (suhṛt). If you've been missing all of those, this verse names them together.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, briefly describing meditation and the peace it brings.
verse_text.line: The divine is the well-wisher of every being, you included. Knowing this, you find peace.
verse_text.translation: Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great lord of all the worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the divine is the friend of all beings, your included, and knowing this brings peace. On days when you do not speak to another adult, this well-wisher remains present in the quiet. Rest in that steady presence here, now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Feel others' joy and pain as if they were your own. That is the highest practice.
verse_text.translation: One who, by comparison with himself, sees the same everywhere, Arjuna, whether in pleasure or in pain, is considered the highest yogi.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to feel others' joy and pain as if they were his own, calling this the highest practice. When your days pass without another adult's voice, you could quietly offer one small kindness to someone today, letting your attention move outward. In doing so, you echo the presence that has stayed with you since the first day.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, describing the qualities of the person dear to God.
verse_text.line: Hate no one. Be friendly and kind, free of 'mine' and ego, steady in pain and joy, and forgiving.
verse_text.translation: One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from possessiveness and ego, even in pain and pleasure, and forgiving,

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the person dear to God hates no one, is friendly and compassionate, free from ego and possessiveness, steady through pain and joy, and forgiving. You could offer one kind word to a stranger today, letting go of who must reach out first. That small step is the practice itself, steady even when no reply comes back.

story.title: Ram and Sugriva become friends
story.summary: Ram had lost his home, and his wife Sita had been taken. Sugriva, driven out by his brother, had lost his home and his wife too. They met in the forest and swore friendship before a fire. Then Sugriva brought out the jewels Sita had dropped as she was carried away. Ram broke down at the sight of them, and Sugriva, who had his own grief, comforted him: in trouble, think it through steadily, and lean on your friend.
story.lesson: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

days.reading: In the Kishkindha Kanda, Ram and Sugriva, both exiled and grieving, swear friendship before a fire. Sugriva comforts Ram with his own loss, showing that two people in trouble can carry each other. You wake in a new country without another adult to speak to; this story points to a shared fire where two broken people sit together and steady one another.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: Krishna says that whoever sees him everywhere, and everything in him, is never lost to him, and he is never lost to them (na praṇaśyati). Loneliness feels like being lost to everyone. This verse names one bond that distance can't break.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is afraid and confused about the war ahead. Krishna is teaching him how to steady his mind through meditation. He tells Arjuna that a person who sees him in every being and sees every being within him will never be separated from him. The bond remains unbroken because the vision itself keeps both together.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You have spent three years working from home and noticed you have no one, with your phone only buzzing for work. Rama's attendant tells King Dasharatha that the prince no longer lights up at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work, but just keeps silent. That quiet stillness mirrors your own withdrawal today, as your days blur into work without connection.
meaning: Rama's attendant speaks to King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Rama has stopped eating properly, stopped laughing, and sits alone. The attendant reports that Rama no longer laughs at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work. He just keeps silent. The verse proposes that this loss of interest is not mere weakness but the first stirring of deeper questions, provided someone helps the person through it. Your withdrawal after three years at home mirrors Rama's stillness. The silence is not a flaw. It is the ground where better questions can begin to form.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You have spent 15 years in a shared room here, with your wife and kids back home, and you video call every night. Krishna tells Arjuna, See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. When the room feels empty after the call, this presence stays in the space around you, so you are never truly alone in that room.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna while teaching him how to meditate and what a settled mind looks like. Arjuna is learning to still his thoughts and steady his attention. Krishna tells him that a person who sees him in every being and sees every being within him will never be separated from him. The teaching is about moderation and bringing the wandering mind back again and again. After your nightly call ends, the room still holds the shape of those you love. This presence remains in the space around you, so you are never truly alone in that room.

verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
