verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You feel unseen even when the house is full. Krishna tells Arjuna that if he sees the divine in everything and everything in the divine, neither is ever lost to the other. In your crowded home today, this means the one who sees you in every corner never loses sight of you, and you are never lost to them.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is afraid of fighting his own kin. Krishna is teaching him how to steady his mind through meditation. He tells Arjuna that a person who sees the divine in all things and all things in the divine will never be separated from that presence. The idea is that mutual seeing creates a bond that loss cannot break. You carry the weight of being unseen inside a home that never empties. This verse names a way of looking that keeps connection alive even when no one turns toward you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You live in a PG with four others yet share no words, and after work you simply watch the roof. Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever sees him everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him, nor he to them. This means even in a crowded room where no one speaks to you, you are still held within a connection that distance cannot break, like the sky above that roof.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching him about meditation and a settled mind. He tells him that the person who sees him in every being and every being in him will never be lost to Krishna, and Krishna will never be lost to that person. Even when you sit alone in a room with four others and hear nothing, you are still held within a connection that distance cannot break.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You are doing your masters in Melbourne and go days without a real conversation. Krishna tells Arjuna, See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. When your days feel quiet, this can mean that no distance can break the bond where you are seen in all and all in you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching him how to meditate and what a settled mind looks like. He tells him that when a person sees him everywhere and sees everything inside him, then he is never lost to that person, and that person is never lost to him. You are far from home and the silence of your days in Melbourne can feel like a wall. This verse speaks of a bond that no distance breaks, once you learn to look again.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
verse_text.translation: It is never born and never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

reading: You are home with your mother while your wife is away and your children live in a hostel. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not killed when the body is. In your quiet house, this means the essence of the one you care for remains untouched by the silence around you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield of after Arjuna collapses in grief over fighting his own kin. Arjuna has just laid down his bow and declared he would rather die than kill his teachers and elders. Krishna replies that the true self within every person was never born and will never die. It does not perish when the body perishes. The self is eternal, ancient, and unchanging, so grief for the body is grief for a garment that is shed, not for what truly lives. Your mother is fading into silence while your wife is away and your children live elsewhere. This verse speaks to the part of her that outlasts the quiet room and the slow forgetting.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You spend your days among colleagues and your off days alone in your room. Krishna tells Arjuna, See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. When your room feels empty, this view can meet you there: the one you seek is already present in the space around you, and you are already held within it.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching him how to settle the mind through meditation. He tells the warrior that a person who sees him in every being and sees every being within him will never be separated from him, and he will never be separated from that person. The distance you feel between your work days and your empty room is not a break in connection. It is a place where you can learn to see the same presence in both.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You spend the day talking to people yet feel unknown. Rama's attendant tells King Dasharatha that the prince no longer laughs at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work, but simply keeps silent. Like that quiet withdrawal, your own stillness after constant conversation may be a sign that the noise no longer reaches you, leaving room for something unnamed to simply be there.
meaning: Rama's attendant speaks to King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Sixteen-year-old Rama has stopped eating, stopped laughing, and sits alone. The attendant reports that the prince no longer reacts to jokes, takes no pleasure in things, and does not stay with his work. He simply keeps silent. Your own withdrawal after constant talking may be the first sign that the noise has stopped reaching you.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: After your fourth UPSC attempt, your courage is fading. Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Like Arjuna, you too can let your weapons rest without forcing yourself forward. Your bow and arrows may also simply lie still today.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid down his bow and sits in his chariot. His mind is overwhelmed by grief. The verse shows that even a great warrior can freeze when sorrow hits. It proposes that a breakdown is a real beginning, not a failure. After your fourth attempt, your courage is fading. Like Arjuna, you can set your weapons down without forcing the next step today.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You have poured everything into two businesses that closed, and now nothing stirs you. The Yoga Vasishtha records Rama's attendant describing the prince: he no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work; he just keeps silent. That quiet withdrawal speaks to your emptiness today. Let your stillness be enough, resting in the fact that you no longer force yourself to stay with what has already ended.
meaning: Rama's attendant speaks to King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Sixteen-year-old Rama has quietly withdrawn. He stops eating, ignores his duties, and sits alone. The attendant reports that Rama no longer laughs at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work. He just keeps silent. The verse proposes that this loss of interest is not mere illness or weakness. It can be the start of asking better questions, provided someone helps the person through it. You poured everything into two businesses that closed, and now the silence where your drive used to be feels like proof that nothing will ever work for you.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You have been trying to lose weight for years and keep failing, and you have basically given up on yourself. In this verse, Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Like Arjuna setting down his bow, your body may be resting after years of effort; today, that same seat of the chariot is simply where you are.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid down his weapons and collapsed in his chariot. He is paralyzed by grief and fear at the thought of fighting his own kin. Sanjaya reports that even the greatest warrior can freeze when his mind is overwhelmed. The verse shows that a breakdown is not a failure of strength but a human response to unbearable weight. After years of trying and failing, your body has settled into stillness. That stillness is not weakness. It is the honest result of carrying too much for too long.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You feel defeated. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. When hope runs low after setbacks, sitting still with that weight is part of the path, not the end of it. Let your bow rest today, and stay in the chariot.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra from the battlefield. Arjuna stands among the armies, ready to fight his own kin. He is overcome by grief and fear. He drops his weapons and sinks onto the chariot seat. The verse records this collapse. It shows that even a mighty warrior can freeze when the cost of action feels too high. You are in that same seat, with the fight paused and the weight of defeat heavy on your chest.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: हर कोशिश नाकाम हो रही है, और अब हार मान लेने का मन कर रहा है। संजया कहते हैं कि अर्जुन ने युद्धभूमि में अपना धनुष गिराकर रथ पर बैठ गए, उनका मन शोक से भर गया। आज भी आप अपनी कोशिशों के बीच इसी तरह रुक सकते हैं; अपने काम के बीच एक पल रुककर अपने धनुष को नीचे रख दें, और बस वहीं बैठे रहें।
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra. On the battlefield, Arjuna has just laid down his weapons and collapsed in his chariot. He is paralyzed by grief and refuses to fight his own kin. The verse records this collapse. It shows that even a mighty warrior can freeze when sorrow overwhelms him. The Gita begins not with courage but with a breakdown.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: After one health problem after another, and now the knee surgery failed too, you have stopped believing you will get better. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Like him, you too can set down what has become too heavy to carry and simply sit with what is real today.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid down his bow and arrows. He sits in the chariot, overcome by grief and confusion. The verse records this moment of collapse. It shows that even a mighty warrior can freeze when the weight becomes too much. Your body has faced one setback after another, and now the knee surgery has failed too. You have stopped believing you will get better.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You keep waiting to restart your work each year, but something always gets in the way, and now hope feels gone. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Today, you too can lay down the weight of that yearly wait and simply sit where you are, with the bow set aside.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between the two armies. He sees his kin and teachers ready to die. Grief and fear grip him. He drops his bow and arrows. He sinks onto the chariot seat. He cannot move. The verse shows a collapse. It says even the strongest freeze when the cost becomes too clear. Your yearly restart has met the same wall again and again. The verse names that freeze without shame.

verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: Poem 'Hold On Yet a While, Brave Heart', written to the Maharaja of Khetri.
verse_text.line: Still hold on yet a while, brave heart, The victory is sure to come.
verse_text.translation: If the sun by the cloud is hidden a bit, If the welkin shows but gloom, Still hold on yet a while, brave heart, The victory is sure to come. … Not a work will be lost, no struggle vain, Though hopes be blighted, powers gone; … Then hold on yet a while, brave soul, No good is e'er undone.

reading: You are carrying a land case that has dragged on for seven years, with every hearing postponed, and you have lost hope of ever getting justice. The verse says, 'Still hold on yet a while, brave heart, The victory is sure to come.' It speaks to your restlessness by trusting that no struggle is vain, even when the sky shows only gloom. You can hold on to this truth while you wait for the next hearing.
meaning: Swami Vivekananda wrote this poem to the Maharaja of Khetri, a friend facing hard times. He tells him that clouds may hide the sun for a while and the sky may show only gloom. Yet he says the victory is sure to come. No honest struggle is wasted, even when hopes fail and powers seem gone. The verse asks the listener to keep holding on a little longer. Your land case has dragged on for seven years and each hearing keeps slipping away. The verse asks you to trust that this long wait is not empty.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: After the fifth rejection on the same paper, you feel you do not have it in you to revise it again. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Like him, you can lay down what you have been carrying and simply sit with the weight of it today.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra from the battlefield. Arjuna has just argued that killing his own kin is not worth any victory. Overcome by grief and delusion, Arjuna lets his bow and arrows fall to the seat of his chariot. He sits down and refuses to fight. The verse records a moment of total collapse. Even a great warrior can freeze when the cost becomes too heavy. You are facing a fifth rejection on the same paper and you feel you have nothing left to give it another revision.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

meaning: Bali speaks this to himself. He is a demon king who has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day he sits by his window and sees that his days and nights repeat the same tasks. He feels that this endless loop mocks any thinking person. The verse proposes that when life feels like a closed circle, the way out is not to add more work but to master the mind that runs the loop. You are facing the same wall no matter how hard you push against it.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You described every plan this year falling apart one after another, leaving you feeling lost. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna, overwhelmed by grief, put down his bow and sank onto the chariot seat. In your own running of things, you too can set down the weight of the next plan and simply sit, letting the bow rest where it is.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra from the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid out his grief and fear. He sees his kin arrayed against him and cannot bear to strike them down. His mind collapses under the weight of that love and dread. He lets his bow and arrows fall and sinks onto the chariot seat, too overwhelmed to continue. You are running your own thing and every plan has collapsed in a row. That collapse has left you feeling lost, as if the ground under your work has given way.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: After sixty rejections, you have set down your pen and stopped writing. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna, the greatest archer, put down his bow and sat in his chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Like him, you may simply be too heavy to go on right now, and that collapse is where the teaching begins.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid down his bow and sat in his chariot. His mind is overwhelmed by grief. He refuses to fight because he cannot bear to kill his own kin. The verse records this collapse. It shows that even the greatest warrior can freeze when the weight becomes too much. You have stopped writing after sixty rejections. That freeze is not a failure of talent. It is the body and mind saying the load is too heavy right now.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You are starting at a new company on the 1st after two years under a terrible manager, seeking a clean slate. Lakshman tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it; for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. Let that steadiness guide you as you step into this new chapter, carrying the hope you already feel into the work ahead.
meaning: At Lake Pampa, after Sita has been taken, Ram is overcome by grief. The beauty of spring only sharpens his sorrow. Lakshman steps in and tells him that enthusiasm is powerful. There is no strength greater than it. For the person who holds it, nothing in the world is out of reach. After two years under a terrible manager, your hope for a clean slate is real. This verse names that hope as a strength you already carry into the new company.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You arrived in Toronto last month full of hope yet feeling scared. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, and as hard to hold as the wind. Your thoughts may keep circling the newness around you, yet the same wind that resists the hand also carries the breath you draw in this city. Notice one steady breath tonight, and let the rest move as it will.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the field before battle. He admits that his mind jumps around and will not stay still. He says it is as hard to control as the wind. Krishna agrees that the mind is restless and strong. He adds that steady practice and letting go can slowly train it. You are in a place where hope and fear share the same room. Arjuna names the same restlessness you feel after a move.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: As you shift into your new home after marriage, Lakshman tells Ram that enthusiasm holds unmatched strength. For the one who carries it, nothing in the world is out of reach. Let this steady energy guide your fresh start, turning the moving boxes and new rooms into proof of what you can reach.
meaning: At Lake Pampa, after Sita is taken, Ram stands in grief while spring blooms around him. Lakshman, his younger brother, sees him falter. He tells Ram that enthusiasm holds unmatched strength. For the person who carries it, no task in the world lies beyond reach. You are starting this new life in a new home, and you want the beginning to be strong.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You are stepping into day one of your organic farm after leaving corporate life behind. Savitri tells her father-in-law, "I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end." As you begin this new chapter tomorrow, let that same resolve guide your hands in the soil and your decisions on the land.
meaning: Savitri speaks to Dyumatsena, her father-in-law, after she learns her husband Satyavan will die within three days. She has begun a hard three night vow to face death itself. She tells him not to be distressed. She says the vow was begun with determination, and determination alone will carry it to the end. She means that steady resolve can sustain a promise even when fear would make someone drop it. You are leaving a long corporate career to begin your own farm tomorrow, and you carry that same resolve into the unknown.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You are starting a whole new chapter this Friday. Lakshman tells Ram that there is no strength greater than enthusiasm, and for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. As you begin this next phase with intention, let that steady enthusiasm guide your first steps forward.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Ram is drowning in grief after Sita is taken. Everything around him is beautiful and only deepens his sorrow. Lakshman, Ram's younger brother, steps in and tells him that enthusiasm is the greatest strength. For the person who holds it, nothing in the world is out of reach. You stand at the edge of this new chapter with hope in your chest. Lakshman's words meet that hope and give it weight.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You are flying to Doha this Sunday for your first job abroad. Lakshman tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it; for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. As you step into this fresh chapter, let that conviction meet the boarding gate and the new city, carrying you forward.
meaning: At Lake Pampa, after Sita has been taken, Ram is surrounded by the beauty of spring and his grief grows heavy. Lakshman, his younger brother, steps in and tells him that enthusiasm holds the greatest strength. For the person who carries it, no goal in the world lies beyond reach. You are about to cross an ocean for work, and that hope is already moving in your chest.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Don't abandon work that suits you just because it has flaws. Every undertaking has some, like fire has smoke.
verse_text.translation: One should not give up the work suited to one's nature, Kaunteya, even if it has faults; for all undertakings are clouded by faults, as fire is by smoke.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that every undertaking is clouded by faults, just as fire is by smoke, so do not abandon work suited to your nature simply because it has flaws. As you begin this first job abroad and fly to Doha, expect small imperfections to appear, but let that steadiness carry you through the week ahead.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Without self-control it's hard. With sincere effort and the right means, it's within reach.
verse_text.translation: Yoga is hard to reach for one whose self is uncontrolled, in my view. But one whose self is controlled and who strives can reach it by the right means.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that yoga is hard for one whose mind is uncontrolled, but reachable for one who strives by the right means. As you begin your first job abroad and fly to Doha, this steadiness gives you ground to stand on. The unfamiliar path feels hard because it is new, yet sincere effort makes it within reach.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: So keep doing the work that needs doing, well and without clinging. That's how you rise.
verse_text.translation: Therefore, always do the work that has to be done, without attachment; by working without attachment a person reaches the highest.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to keep doing the work that needs doing, well and without clinging, because that is how one rises. As you settle into your first job abroad, this steadiness gives you ground to stand on while the newness fades. Let your focus rest on doing today’s tasks well, without obsessing over how the whole journey will turn out.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: Cut the doubt in your heart with clear understanding, then stand up and act.
verse_text.translation: Therefore, cutting with the sword of knowledge this doubt in your heart born of ignorance, take refuge in yoga, and stand up, Bharata.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to cut the doubt in his heart with the sword of clear understanding, then stand up and act. As you begin this new job abroad, doubt may visit you, but you do not have to wait for it to leave. You could write down one fact you know about this role today, then take the first step.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna, as Time, tells Arjuna the outcome is already set and urges him to act.
verse_text.line: It's already set in motion. Rise and do your part; be the instrument.
verse_text.translation: Therefore stand up and win glory; conquer your enemies and enjoy a prosperous kingdom. They have already been slain by me; be merely the instrument, ambidextrous archer.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the larger outcome is already in motion and urges him to rise and play his part, being merely the instrument. As you fly to Doha for your first job abroad, you could embrace this by showing up fully for one small task today, trusting you are part of something bigger.

story.title: Satyakama Jabala
story.summary: Young Satyakama wanted to study, but he didn't know his father's lineage. He told the teacher exactly what his mother had told him. The teacher accepted him for that honesty and handed him four hundred weak, thin cows to look after. Satyakama said he wouldn't come back until they were a thousand. He spent years in the forest, and returned with a thousand cows and a mind that nature itself had taught.
story.lesson: Start honestly, start small, and stay with it.

days.reading: Satyakama tells his teacher he does not know his father's lineage, and the teacher accepts his honesty, giving him four hundred weak cows to tend. You are beginning a new chapter far from home, and this story shows that starting with what you actually know, and with a small, fragile step, can grow into something far larger than you began. You carry those thin cows with you into Doha, and you will not return until they have become a thousand.

reading: With your first child arriving next month and a new life beginning, Lakshman tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful and no strength exceeds it. This steadiness can meet the wonder you feel right now. Let that inner drive carry you through the first days ahead.

Lakshman steps in and tells him that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it. For the person who carries it, nothing in the world is out of reach. As you wait for your first child next month, this steadiness meets the wonder you feel right now.

reading: You got into a good college after a drop year and want to start this chapter right. Lakshman tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it; for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. Your inspiration right now is exactly that kind of energy. Let it carry you into your first semester.
meaning: At the lake of Pampa in spring, Ram is grieving Sita's absence and the beauty around him only deepens his sorrow. Lakshman sees his brother falter and speaks to him directly. He says that enthusiasm holds the greatest strength of all. For the person who carries it, no goal in the world lies beyond reach. Your inspiration now is that same force Lakshman names. It can carry the weight of your first semester without asking you to prove it yet.

reading: You moved to a new country at 62 to live near your children and start over. Lakshman tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it, so for the one who has it nothing is out of reach. story.title: Pingala's song
story.summary: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira about Pingala, who sat awake one night waiting for a lover who never came. Every sound outside might have been his footsteps, so she kept listening. Late in the night she saw what was keeping her awake. It was her hope that someone else would arrive and settle her. She let that hope go, and she slept peacefully.
story.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.

days.reading: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira about Pingala, who stayed awake waiting for a lover who never arrived, until she realized her sleeplessness came from hoping someone else would settle her. Letting go of the hope that another outcome will finally quiet your mind can bring the sleep that waiting never will.

The verse proposes that even a mighty warrior can break down when the cost of action becomes clear. It begins with a collapse, not a charge. Your body is answering the same pressure. verse_text.speaker: Krishna

verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You have two years left before retirement, and now you carry the biggest project of your career with daily pressure. meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna collapses in grief on the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid down his weapons and said he cannot fight his own kin. He says contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These experiences come and go and do not last. He asks Arjuna to bear them patiently. The pressure you feel at work is part of a passing contact between your senses and the task before you. It will come and go, and it does not define what you truly are.

verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?

verse_text.translation: Hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance belong to one born with the demonic nature, Partha.

verse_text.line: Free of clinging and boasting, full of resolve and enthusiasm, unchanged by success or failure: the best kind of doer.
verse_text.translation: The doer who is free from attachment, does not speak of himself, is full of steadiness and enthusiasm, and unmoved by success or failure, is called sattvic.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the best doer is free from clinging and boasting, full of resolve, and unchanged by success or failure. story.title: Nahusha's fall
story.summary: King Nahusha was so successful that he was made ruler of heaven. Drunk on it, he made sages carry his palanquin and kicked one to hurry him along. The sage cursed him, and he fell to earth as a giant python. Ages later he seized Bhima in the forest, and was freed only after Yudhishthira answered his questions about what makes a person good.
story.lesson: Success can blind anyone. Conduct is what makes a person good.

days.reading: Nahusha became ruler of heaven yet grew drunk on success and kicked a sage to hurry his palanquin, falling to earth as a python. Your rise has drawn people to your advice, yet the same success can blind you to your own conduct. Let your conduct, not your hype, shape how you carry this new weight.

verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: Six days a week on site, then room, then site again. The Yoga Vasishtha records Bali saying that day and night bring the same chain of tasks, and a thinking person feels mocked by it. Your body is tired in a way rest does not touch. In that repetition, the verse sees a mockery; let Bali's words sit beside your own six-day loop.
meaning: Bali is a demon king who has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day he sits by his window and watches the same cycle of day and night. He speaks to himself. He says the same tasks return again and again. To a thinking person this repetition feels like a mockery. Your six day loop of site and room echoes Bali's endless chain. The verse names the same mockery you feel in your bones.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse_text.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse_text.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.

reading: You are on an H1B with a restructuring announced and 60 days to find something. Arjuna tells Krishna, 'My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.' Your body is already showing the same signs of panic. Notice where your feet are right now, and let that grounding hold you.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He sees his own relatives arrayed against him. His body fails him. The verse lists the physical signs of collapse. Limbs give way. The mouth goes dry. The body trembles. The hair stands on end. It proposes that a breakdown is a valid starting point, not a failure of strength. Your body is already sounding the alarm before your mind has settled on a plan.

verse_text.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.

reading: Your payment is stuck in the market, the supplier calls daily, and your shop rent is still pending. Arjuna tells Krishna, "My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end." That same shaking in the body belongs to you today, not as a sign of weakness but as the honest start of facing what feels unsafe.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He sees his own kin lined up in the enemy ranks. His body fails him. His limbs give way, his mouth goes dry, his body trembles, and his hair stands on end. The verse shows that the teaching begins with this collapse, not with courage. The same physical shock you carry right now is where any real response begins, not a flaw in your strength.

That shaking body belongs to someone facing an uncertain future, and your own dry mouth and racing pulse are simply the body speaking the truth of this unsafe moment.

The verse records a complete physical collapse. It proposes that even a warrior of great strength can freeze when faced with a terrible choice. Your racing body and dry mouth are not a failure; they are the plain report of a leader facing sudden collapse. At 3am, let your trembling limbs simply be the truth you carry into the next meeting.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: Your cafe has been open for a year, and each month brings a loss while your savings are almost gone. Sanjaya says Arjuna sank down in his chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief. You too can lay down the weight of this running for a moment, and simply sit with the loss in front of you.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra from the battlefield. Arjuna stands among the armies and sees his own kin ready to fight. Grief and fear grip him. He drops his bow and arrows and sinks onto his chariot seat. He cannot move forward. The verse shows a collapse. It says even the strongest person can freeze when the weight is too much. Your cafe has run for a year and the losses keep coming while your savings run low. You are not weak for feeling stuck. You are simply facing a moment where the weight outruns the will to push on.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna calls these mātrā-sparśa: contacts, things that touch you and move on. A deadline, a bad week, a hard meeting. They hurt while they last, they pass, and Krishna asks you to bear them (titikṣasva) until they do.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Without inner discipline there's no clarity; without clarity, no peace; and without peace, where is happiness?
verse_text.translation: For the undisciplined there is no understanding and no steady contemplation. Without contemplation there is no peace, and for the one without peace, where is happiness?

days.reading: Krishna lays out a chain. An unsettled mind has no clarity, without clarity there is no peace, and without peace there is no happiness, however good things look on paper. The workload is one part of stress. The other part is a mind with no place to stand.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on working in the world without being stained by it.
verse_text.line: Like a lotus leaf in water, do your work without letting the mess soak in.
verse_text.translation: One who acts offering all actions to the Supreme, giving up attachment, is not touched by wrong, as a lotus leaf is not wet by water.

days.reading: A lotus leaf sits in water all its life, and the water still beads and rolls off it. Krishna uses it for someone who works fully and lets the mess around them roll off. You stay in the pond and keep your surface dry.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Rivers pour into the ocean and it stays full and still. Let desires enter you the same way.
verse_text.translation: As waters enter the ocean, which is ever being filled yet stays unmoved within its shores, so the one into whom all desires enter in the same way finds peace, not the one who craves desires.

days.reading: Rivers keep pouring into the ocean and it stays full and still. Demands will keep coming. In Krishna's picture, peace comes from being deep enough to take them in.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Moderate in food and rest, in work and play, in sleep and waking: that's how sorrow eases.
verse_text.translation: For one who is moderate in food and recreation, measured in effort at work, moderate in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.

days.reading: This is the Gita at its most practical. Krishna tells Arjuna that the yoga which ends sorrow belongs to someone moderate in food, movement, work, sleep and waking. A lot of stress starts as a schedule with no rest built into it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse_text.line: Hand your work to something higher, drop the 'mine' and the hoping, and act with the fever gone.
verse_text.translation: Surrendering all actions to me, with your mind on the inner self, free from hope and the sense of 'mine', fight with your fever gone.

days.reading: The Sanskrit is vigata-jvaraḥ: with the fever gone. Krishna still wants Arjuna to fight, and to fight without the heat of 'mine' and anxious hoping. Offer the work to something larger than your worry, and do it.

story.title: Janaka on the palace roof
story.summary: Walking in his garden one spring, King Janaka overheard hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbed to his palace roof and questioned everything he had lived for. When his attendant came to call him to the day's work, he could have walked away from the throne. He didn't. He went back and did his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutched.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

days.reading: When stress builds, it's tempting to dream of quitting everything. Janaka kept the same work and held it differently.

Krishna hears Arjuna tell him that his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, and his body trembles. In the same way, your anxiety right now is a real bodily response, not a failure, and the teaching begins exactly where you stand today.

It names the physical reality of fear before any teaching begins. Your anxiety right now is a real bodily response to real pressure, not a failure of character, and the teaching begins exactly where you stand today.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You are carrying the hurt of your boss tearing down your report in front of everyone. Bhartrihari tells his own hope that he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart, folding his hands before those numbed by money. Today, your own report being called bakwas in public echoes that same empty performance, and your hurt is the real weight behind the laughter you were forced to show.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to his own hope from the section on craving. He confesses that he endured the mockery of cruel people while trying to please them. He held back his tears and laughed with an empty heart. He even folded his hands before those whose minds were numbed by money. He asks his hope how much longer it will make him dance in this futile way. Your boss tearing down your report in front of everyone puts you in that same empty performance. The hurt you feel is the weight behind the forced reaction you had to show.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You have been acting head for two years, and now a younger man from outside has been hired for the permanent role. Arjuna tells Krishna that his nature is stricken by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right, and he asks plainly to be taught. Your unease today meets the same honest admission: you do not know the path forward, and that uncertainty is itself a clear starting point.
meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield. He has collapsed in tears and refuses to fight. He tells Krishna that his nature is stricken by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right. He asks Krishna to tell him for certain what is best. He calls himself Krishna's student and says he has come to be taught. Your unease meets the same honest admission. You do not know the path forward, and that uncertainty is itself a clear starting point.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You feel angry because your ideas only get heard when a guy repeats them in the meeting. Bhartrihari tells you that if you stay quiet you are dull, but if you speak up you are a show-off, and serving a boss is harder than yoga. This verse sees the bind you are in, where any move you make is twisted. Today, you might notice that same trap when your own words are passed off as someone else's.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari

reading: After ten years of effort, the promotion went to someone else and you feel unseen. Bhartrihari cries out to hope, saying he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart while trying to please others. Your forced smile at work carries that same hollow weight today. Let the verse sit with the quiet ache behind your laughter.

He held back his tears and folded his hands before those numbed by money. He asks hope how much longer it will make him dance. You gave ten years and the reward went elsewhere. Bhartrihari names the hollow weight of pleasing others while your own worth is ignored.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

reading: You feel overlooked while others get ahead. Krishna says it is better to follow your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly. Your own work, done in tune with who you are, carries its own worth. Let your own effort be the measure you stand by today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield of after Arjuna has laid down his weapons in despair. Krishna lists the duties that belong to different ways of life. Then he tells Arjuna that perfection comes from doing the work that matches his own nature. Even if that work is flawed, it is better than performing another person's duty perfectly. Every path has its rough edges. Your own effort has worth even when others around you move ahead faster.

Bhartrihari writes that if you stay quiet you are dull, if you speak up you are a show-off, and serving a master is harder than yoga. This verse sees that exact trap: no response you make will win fair treatment from him. The concrete reality is that his staff watches while he withholds your pay, and that public dismissal is the cost of the work you have already done.

reading: Your director nitpicks your work while praising identical submissions from others, and you dread Monday mornings. Bhartrihari cries out to hope: he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart, folding his hands before those numbed by money. You too have held back tears to please people who misread your modesty as weakness. Today, you can stop forcing the laugh and let your hands rest empty.

He admits he swallowed insults, forced laughter with an empty heart, and folded his hands before people numbed by wealth. He asks how much longer hope will make him dance. You have folded your hands before a director who misreads your work, and you have held back your tears to keep the peace. The verse names what you have already done.

Keep away and you lack confidence. Be patient and you are weak. Refuse to tolerate abuse and you are ill bred. Your TL took credit for your work in front of the client. Bhartrihari names the trap where any response you make can be twisted into a fault.

reading: You carry two decades of experience from India, yet now you report to someone half your age. Bhartrihari speaks this truth: keep quiet and you are dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga. Today, your long record sits unseen beside a younger superior, and every response feels like a trap. Let the verse hold that weight: your position is genuinely impossible, not a flaw in you.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks from the section on the wicked. He addresses anyone who serves a master. He lists the trap. Speak and you are a windbag. Stay silent and you are dull. Stay close and you are pushy. Keep away and you lack confidence. Be patient and you are weak. Refuse and you are ill bred. The duty of serving another is deep. It is beyond the reach even of yogis. Your two decades of experience count for nothing in this room. The verse names the trap you are in, not a flaw in you.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.

reading: You feel overlooked again. Bhartrihari tells you that keeping quiet makes you dull, while speaking up makes you a show-off; being patient makes you weak, and refusing to tolerate things makes you ill-bred. This impossible tightrope speaks to your anger today, because no matter which way you turn at work, you are judged. The verse simply names the trap you are caught in, and your next step can be to notice exactly which of these labels was thrown at you most recently.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks from a section on the wicked. He addresses anyone who serves a master. No matter what the servant does, the master twists it into a fault. Keeping silence brings the charge of dullness. Speaking well brings the charge of being a babbler. Staying close brings the charge of being pushy. Keeping away brings the charge of lacking confidence. Patience brings the charge of cowardice. Refusal to tolerate things brings the charge of being ill-bred. The duty of serving another is therefore a deep trap, beyond the reach even of those who practice yoga. At work you are caught in this same trap, where every move is reframed as a flaw.
