reading: You feel caught because your manager talks over you yet questions your silence. Bhartrihari tells the reader that if you keep quiet you are called dull, and if you speak you are called a show-off. This verse names the impossible trap you are in today, where any response is misread, and it points to the real difficulty of serving under such a boss.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks from the section on the wicked to anyone who serves a master. He lists the impossible judgments a person faces. Keep quiet and you are dull. Speak well and you are a babbler. Stay close and you are pushy. Keep away and you lack confidence. Be patient and you are a coward. Refuse to put up with things and you are ill bred. He concludes that serving another carries a duty so deep it lies beyond the reach even of yogis. Your manager turns every response into a fault. The verse shows that this trap belongs to the boss, not to your silence.

verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: 'My Plan of Campaign', Madras, February 1897, on friends who turned critics.
verse_text.line: as soon as he dares to differ, that sympathy is gone, that love vanishes.
verse_text.translation: We hear so much tall talk in this world, of liberal ideas and sympathy with differences of opinion. That is very good, but as a fact, we find that one sympathises with another only so long as the other believes in everything he has to say, but as soon as he dares to differ, that sympathy is gone, that love vanishes.

reading: You are running your own thing and feel hurt. Swami Vivekananda says that love vanishes as soon as one dares to differ. In your investor meeting, the co-founder took the credit alone, and that silence from someone close can sting deeply today. You can sit with that loss of support as it is.
meaning: Swami Vivekananda speaks these words to an audience at Victoria Hall in Madras during February 1897. He is responding to critics who claimed others made his success in America. He notes that people often talk about liberal sympathy for differing views. Yet in practice, they only support someone while that person agrees with everything they say. The moment the other person dares to differ, the sympathy disappears and the love vanishes. Your co-founder took the credit alone in the investor meeting, and that sudden withdrawal of support from someone close mirrors exactly what Vivekananda describes.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You carry the ache of words that never came. Rama tells Kaikeyi that the deepest wound was not the exile itself, but that his father did not tell him the news himself. That silence still burns in your heart today, even after the wedding speech passed. Let that unnamed sorrow sit with you, not as a debt to settle, but as a truth you already know.
meaning: Rama speaks these words to Kaikeyi after he has calmly accepted fourteen years of exile in the forest. Kaikeyi had demanded his banishment on the morning of his coronation so that her son Bharata could take the throne. Rama agrees without anger and begins to think of how to comfort those he leaves behind. Yet one thing still burns in him. He tells Kaikeyi that the deepest sorrow is not the exile itself, but that his father did not tell him the news with his own voice. Your father spoke at your wedding about your brother instead of you. That gap between what you hoped to hear and what was said still sits in your chest.

verse_text.speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
verse_text.setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
verse_text.line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.
verse_text.translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.

reading: You feel utterly alone even though you have your husband. Sita tells Ram through Hanuman, 'I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.' Your heart knows this gap between being with someone and truly being seen by them. When his family speaks behind your back and he stays silent, let Sita's words sit with you as a quiet witness to that isolation.
meaning: Sita speaks this to Rama through Hanuman. She has been held captive in Lanka for months. She tells Rama that he is her protector and that he belongs to her. Yet she says she looks like a person with no one at all. The verse names the gap between having a protector and feeling utterly alone. You carry a marriage that looks complete from the outside but leaves you unseen at home.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: Your heart feels churned like a fire-stick, Krishna says, because harsh words from family keep burning day after day. You carry the weight of being called a burden. This verse names that inner fire as real, not as your failing, and points to the very words that still sting inside you today.
meaning: Bhishma tells the sage Narada that Krishna once confessed his own heart was churned like a fire-stick. Krishna said his relatives spoke harsh words that kept burning him day after day. The verse proposes that in family feuds the only working weapon is softness, patience and respect. You carry the weight of being called a burden, and those words still sting inside you today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You gave up your career to care for your mum, yet your siblings claim you only did it for the house. Krishna tells Narada that harsh words from relatives keep burning him day after day. Like his fire-stick, your hurt still burns, and that pain is real today.
meaning: Bhishma tells Narada that Krishna once spoke of his own heart. Krishna had grown tired of feuds inside his own clan. He asked the sage how to keep the peace. Krishna said his heart felt churned like a fire-stick being rubbed to spark flame. He said the harsh words his relatives spoke kept burning him day after day. The point is that in family feuds, the only weapon that works is gentleness, patience and respect. Your siblings say you cared for the house, not your mother. That accusation still burns, and the pain is real.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: Krishna tells Narada that harsh words from relatives keep burning him day after day. You gave money home for 15 years, yet your brother says you never did anything for the family. Like Krishna, you can carry the burn of those words without letting them define what you built.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing weary of feuds within his own clan. He describes how the harsh words of relatives keep burning him long after they are spoken. The verse proposes that in family conflicts, the only effective weapon is not force but gentleness, patience and respect. You gave money home for fifteen years and now hear that you did nothing. The verse shows that such words can keep burning a person even when they know the truth.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing weary of quarrels inside his own clan. He admits that the harsh words spoken by his relatives continue to wound him long after they are spoken. He compares his own heart to a fire-stick being churned by someone who wants flame. The verse proposes that in family conflict, the only effective weapon is not force but gentleness, patience and respect.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has lain on the shore for three days asking the ocean for a way across. No answer comes.
verse_text.line: Calm, patience, honesty and kind words: people who don't value them will read them as weakness.
verse_text.translation: See the ocean's arrogance: he does not even show himself. Calm, forbearance, straightforwardness and gentle speech, these virtues of the good, are taken by the unworthy as signs of weakness.

verse_text.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse_text.speaker: Prahlada (quoted by Draupadi)
verse_text.setting: Draupadi quotes old Prahlada answering his grandson: is forgiveness better, or force?
verse_text.line: Force isn't always right, and forgiveness isn't always right. Wisdom is knowing which the moment needs.
verse_text.translation: Force is not always best, and forgiveness is not always best. Know this for certain, my child: both have their place.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Uttanka, furious that the war happened, threatens to curse Krishna for not stopping it.
verse_text.line: I tried hard to make peace. When people refuse to be reconciled, you can't force it.
verse_text.translation: I made every effort earlier to bring the Kauravas to peace. But they could not be brought to agree, however I tried.

days.reading: Krishna tells the furious sage Uttanka that he tried hard to bring the Kauravas to peace, but they simply refused to agree. You do not have to carry the weight of forcing harmony when harsh words keep coming. Let this ground stand beneath you today: your peace is not your task to force.

verse_text.speaker: Seer
verse_text.setting: The creation story: last of all, dharma is made.
verse_text.line: Nothing is higher than what is right. With it the weak can face the strong. What is right is truth.
verse_text.translation: Still he did not flourish. So he created a higher form, dharma. Dharma is the power over power; nothing is higher than dharma. Through dharma even a weak man can stand up to a strong one, as with the help of a king. That dharma is truth. So people say of one who speaks truth, 'He speaks dharma,' and of one who speaks dharma, 'He speaks truth.' Both are the same.

days.reading: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says that nothing is higher than what is right, and through it even a weak person can stand up to a strong one. You could let this idea guide one small choice today, standing firmly on what is right even when harsh words come. This echoes Day 1, where even Krishna felt the burn of family words.

verse_text.speaker: Kabandha
verse_text.setting: Ram is lost and grieving; Kabandha tells him to seek Sugriva, who has also lost his wife and home.
verse_text.line: Find a friend who knows your kind of trouble. You won't get through this alone.
verse_text.translation: You must make him your friend, best of friends. Thinking it over, I see no success for you without it.

days.reading: Kabandha tells the grieving Rama to seek Sugriva, who has also lost his wife and home, and to make him a friend. You could reach out to one classmate who understands this kind of hurt today. You do not carry this alone.

story.title: Hanuman finds a friend in Lanka
story.summary: Searching Lanka, Hanuman is surprised to find a house with Ram's name on it. Its owner, Vibhishan, Ravana's brother, says he lives in Lanka like a tongue among teeth. Hanuman tells him even a restless monkey like himself was given Ram's love.
story.lesson: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.

days.reading: Hanuman finds Vibhishan, Ravana’s brother, living inside Lanka like a tongue among teeth, unable to share his true values with those around him. Vibhishan calls himself lowly and without practice, yet speaking with Hanuman brings him rest. This speaks to your hurt, showing how one true friendship among people who do not understand you can bring relief even before any change happens.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You feel like a stranger in your own home because harsh words from your in-laws keep burning you, day after day. Krishna himself told Narada that such words churn the heart like a fire-stick. You can carry this truth with you today: the fire they lit is real, and it is not yours to feed.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing weary of feuds within his own clan. He describes how the harsh words his relatives speak continue to burn him long after they are spoken. The verse proposes that in family conflict, the only effective weapon is not force but gentleness, patience and respect. Your in-laws' criticism and your husband's dismissal are real wounds that keep reopening, just as Krishna described.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You feel lost after being betrayed by your own family. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in his chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Like him, you can lay down the weight you are carrying right where you are, without forcing yourself forward.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid down his weapons and collapsed in his chariot, paralyzed by grief and confusion. He sees his own kin arrayed against him and cannot bring himself to fight. Sanjaya reports that the great warrior simply sat down, letting his bow and arrows fall, his mind overwhelmed by sorrow. You are facing a collapse that feels sudden and total, after the people closest to you turned against you.

verse_text.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, CIII, p. 160
verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: Letter from Belur, 18 May 1901, ill and grieving the sudden death of the Raja of Khetri.
verse_text.line: Yet I am sure to bob up soon and am waiting for the next turn.
verse_text.translation: The Raja of Khetri died from a fall a few months ago. So you see things are all gloomy with me just now, and my own health is wretched. Yet I am sure to bob up soon and am waiting for the next turn.

days.reading: Swami Vivekananda writes from Belur that despite gloomy circumstances and wretched health, he is sure to bob up soon and is waiting for the next turn. From the verse's view, this buoyancy does not deny the darkness but trusts that a turn will come. You, sitting in your own low moment after betrayal, can let yourself wait for that next turn without forcing it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what becomes of someone who tries and fails; Krishna reassures him.
verse_text.line: Whoever does good never comes to ruin, my friend. Not here, not after.
verse_text.translation: The Blessed Lord said: Partha, there is no ruin for him either in this world or the next. No one who does good, my friend, ever comes to grief.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever does good never comes to ruin, here or after. After your own family betrayed you, this means the good you have tried to do has not been wasted. You can stand on the fact that your efforts remain intact, even when hope feels low.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on worship for rewards and worship without desire.
verse_text.line: Turn to me with your whole heart, and I will carry what you lack and guard what you have.
verse_text.translation: To those who think of me alone and worship me, ever devoted, I bring what they lack and preserve what they have.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that he will carry what they lack and guard what they have when they turn to him with their whole heart. After the weight of betrayal, this invites you to stop carrying everything alone, even while practical plans still move forward. Let this be the ground beneath your feet today: what is missing is held, and what remains is kept.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to lift himself by his own self and not let himself sink, for the self alone is the friend and the enemy of the self. After betrayal by your own family, you could speak one kind sentence to yourself today, treating your own voice as the ally Krishna describes rather than the force that pushes you down.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Yoga is unhooking from sorrow. Practise it with resolve and a heart that doesn't lose hope.
verse_text.translation: Know that to be yoga: the breaking of contact with sorrow. This yoga should be practised with determination and with an undespairing mind.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that yoga is unhooking from sorrow, and to practise it with resolve and a heart that doesn't lose hope. You could sit for a few minutes today and gently notice where sorrow sits, without pushing it away. Let that small pause be your resolve, keeping your mind from giving up.

story.title: Ram waits out the monsoon
story.summary: After Sita was taken, the rains came, and Ram had to wait four months on a mountainside before any search could begin. Nothing could be done. He couldn't sleep for grief. Lakshman sat with him and reminded him that endless grieving drains every purpose, and that this was a season for waiting, not for giving up. Ram resolved to wait well, and when the rains ended, the search began.
story.lesson: Some seasons are for waiting. Wait well, without letting grief take you.

days.reading: After Sita was taken, Ram had to wait four months on a mountainside while the monsoon stopped every search. Lakshman told him that endless grieving drains purpose, so this was a season for waiting, not for giving up, and Ram resolved to wait well until the rains ended. You, too, are in a season where action is paused, and your grief is real; let this waiting be a place where you hold on until the next step opens.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You trusted a friend with your business and were stabbed in the back. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, then desire, and then anger. The verse speaks to the flare inside you today by naming the fire that builds before the snap, pointing to the very moment your mind kept returning to what was broken.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna what a steady person looks like. Krishna answers that such a person is content within and unshaken by sorrow. Then Krishna traces the opposite path. When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and from desire, when it is blocked, anger arises. Your flare today has a beginning point, and it starts in the mind before the body reacts.

verse_text.speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
verse_text.setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
verse_text.line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.
verse_text.translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.

reading: You carry a silence that has lasted two years since your daughter stopped speaking to you after a disagreement about her marriage. Sita tells Ram, "I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one." Even when someone remains close in spirit, the absence of daily words can leave you feeling utterly alone. Let Ram's image of her standing without visible support meet the quiet of your own mornings.
meaning: Sita speaks these words to Rama through Hanuman. She has been held captive in Lanka for months. She knows Rama is her protector and still hers. Yet she says she looks like a person with no one at all. The verse holds the gap between belonging and feeling abandoned. You know your daughter still exists in the world. The silence after your disagreement still makes you feel as though no one stands beside you.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You feel hurt because your parents take your brother's side and dismiss your feelings as drama. Ram says, "Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation." Today, this speaks to you in the silence around your pain: the deepest hurt is not just the taking of sides, but that those closest to you do not meet you with honest acknowledgment. You carry the weight of that unspoken truth.
meaning: Ram speaks to Kaikeyi after he has accepted fourteen years in the forest. He has agreed without anger. Yet one thing still burns him. He tells her that the only sorrow left is that his father did not tell him himself about Bharata's coronation. He accepts the exile. He accepts the loss of his throne. What he cannot accept is the silence of the one who should have spoken first.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You carry the weight of being laughed at after your elder brother humiliated you at a family wedding. Krishna tells Narada that harsh words from relatives keep burning him day after day, just as fire-sticks are churned. Today, that lingering heat in your chest is real. Let it be the fire-stick Krishna names, still burning, without asking you to carry it anywhere yet.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing weary of feuds within his own clan. He describes how the harsh words of his relatives continue to burn inside him, much like a fire-stick that is repeatedly churned to keep a flame alive. The verse proposes that in family conflicts, the only effective weapon is not force but gentleness, patience and respect. Your brother's words and the laughter that followed are still hot inside you, long after the wedding ended.

verse_text.speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
verse_text.setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
verse_text.line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.
verse_text.translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.

reading: You are facing your first real breakup after being together through high school, and now she is at a different college. Sita tells Ram, 'I have you, and yet I look like someone who has no one.' That same ache of being close to someone yet feeling entirely alone can sit with you today as you study. Let Ram's presence remind you that you are not defined by this absence.
meaning: Sita speaks this to Ram through Hanuman while held captive in Lanka. She tells him she has him as her protector, yet she appears to the world as someone with no one at all. The verse holds the gap between having a bond and feeling utterly alone. You are learning that being with someone does not stop the loneliness from arriving.

verse_text.speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
verse_text.setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
verse_text.line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.
verse_text.translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.

reading: You feel empty even though your children still come to you. Sita tells Ram that she has someone who is hers, and still she feels like a person with no one at all. The house echoes when the kids are away, yet your own presence remains with them. That truth stays with you even in the quiet rooms.
meaning: Sita sends this message to Ram through Hanuman while she is held captive in Lanka. She tells him that she still has him as her protector. Yet she feels as though she has no one at all. The verse names a truth about belonging that does not erase the ache of being alone.

verse_text.speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
verse_text.setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
verse_text.line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.
verse_text.translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.

reading: Your twenty years of marriage have ended, leaving you in an empty home. Sita tells Ram, "I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all." Even with a bond that once existed, the silence of that house can echo this same emptiness today. You might sit in that quiet room and let this verse sit with you, naming the ache without trying to fill it.
meaning: Sita speaks to Ram through Hanuman after months of captivity in Lanka. She tells him she has a protector who is hers, yet she appears to the world as someone utterly alone. The verse names the gap between having a bond and feeling abandoned, even when the other person still exists. After twenty years, the house still holds the shape of a shared life, yet the silence makes the bond feel distant.

verse_text.speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
verse_text.setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
verse_text.line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.
verse_text.translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.

reading: You have been married nine years in the same bed, yet you live in different worlds and do not even fight anymore. Sita says, "I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one." This speaks to your loneliness today: even with a partner beside you, the absence of true connection can leave you feeling utterly alone.
meaning: Sita speaks this while held captive in Lanka, sending her message to Rama through Hanuman. She tells him that she has him as her protector, yet she looks as though she has no one at all. The verse names the pain of having a bond on paper while true companionship is missing. You have shared a bed for nine years, but the distance between you makes that presence feel like absence.

verse_text.speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
verse_text.setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
verse_text.line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.
verse_text.translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.

reading: You stand at the same crossroads while he married someone else. Sita tells Ram, "I have you, and yet I look like someone with no one." That mismatch between having a protector and feeling utterly alone speaks directly to where you are today. Let Ram's great-hearted kindness meet you right there at that unchanged spot.
meaning: Sita speaks this to Rama through Hanuman. She has been held captive in Lanka for months. She tells him that she possesses him as her protector, yet she appears to the world as a woman with no one at all. The verse holds the gap between belonging and feeling abandoned. You are at the same unchanged spot while he married someone else. The gap between having him in your past and feeling alone now is exactly what Sita names.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: You are carrying a hurt because your wife took the children and went to India, saying she will not return. Ram says that telling one's grief lightens it a little, yet he asks whom he can tell, for no one knows this ache. Your own heart alone holds the truth of what you shared. Let those words sit with you today.
meaning: Ram speaks to Sita through Hanuman. Sita sits captive, threatened by Ravana, and has nearly lost hope. Only the guard Trijata has shown her kindness. Hanuman drops Ram's ring from a tree and tells her Ram's whole story. Sita calls Ram her ship in a sea of separation. Ram sends word that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet asks whom he can tell, for no one knows this ache. Only his own heart knows the truth of the love between them. Your own heart alone holds the truth of what you shared with her. No one else carries that exact weight.

verse_text.speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
verse_text.setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
verse_text.line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.
verse_text.translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.

reading: You are missing your ex. Sita tells Ram, 'I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.' That ache of having someone yet feeling entirely alone is real for you today. Let that truth sit with you as you move through your working days.
meaning: Sita speaks these words to Ram. She sends this message through Hanuman. She has been held captive in Lanka for months. She knows Ram is her protector and belongs to her. Yet she says she looks like someone with no one at all. She asks Ram to show his great kindness. The verse names a gap between being owned and being seen. It says protection on its own does not fill the room. You miss your ex. That missing can sit right next to the fact that someone else is in your life now.

verse_text.speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
verse_text.setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
verse_text.line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.
verse_text.translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.

reading: You are searching the last few years for the exact moment the love slipped away, yet cannot find it. Sita says, 'I have you, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.' Even while held close, the heart can carry a vast emptiness. Let that truth sit with you as you face the house being sold.
meaning: Sita speaks these words to Rama while held captive in Lanka, sending her message through Hanuman. She tells Rama that he is her protector and he is hers, yet she appears to the world as someone utterly alone. The verse names a stark truth. A person can possess the one they love and still carry the weight of total abandonment. Sita had Rama even while she was locked away. You have your partner even while she says the love is gone. The absence can live inside the presence.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: You had a thirteen-year bond that ended with a single block. Ram tells Sita that speaking pain lightens it, yet asks whom he can tell, since only his own heart knows this ache. Perhaps your heart knows this truth too, carrying the weight of those years in silence.
meaning: In the Sundar Kand of the Ramcharitmanas, Hanuman reaches Sita while she is held captive by Ravana. She has nearly lost hope. Hanuman gives her Ram's ring and tells her Ram's whole story. Ram's message to her says that speaking of pain lightens it a little. But Ram asks whom he can tell, since no one else knows this ache. Only his own heart knows the truth of the love between them. You are carrying a silence that holds thirteen years of something real, ended by a single block.

verse_text.speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
verse_text.setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
verse_text.line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.
verse_text.translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.

reading: You feel empty even though you now have someone who is yours. Sita tells Ram through Hanuman, "I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one." This verse names the ache of holding on while feeling utterly alone. You might carry this heaviness today as a quiet witness to what remains.
meaning: Sita speaks this while held captive in Lanka. She sends it through Hanuman to Ram. She tells him that she has him as her protector. Yet she still looks like a person with no one at all. The verse names a gap between having a bond and feeling any comfort from it. You signed those papers today and the space around you still feels hollow, even though a tie remains.

verse_text.speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
verse_text.setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
verse_text.line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.
verse_text.translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.

reading: You are carrying the weight of his leaving while your daughter still asks about him. Sita tells Ram, "I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one." Even when someone remains close in spirit, the ache of absence can feel total. Let her small question be a quiet place where that truth is held, not solved.
meaning: Sita speaks to Ram through Hanuman. She has been held captive in Lanka for months. She reminds Ram that he is her protector and still hers. Yet she says she looks like a person with no one at all. She asks him to show his great kindness. The verse says that even when someone remains yours, absence can make you feel entirely alone. You still hold him as yours in some way, and your daughter still calls him papa. Yet the leaving has made you feel as though no one is truly there.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

meaning: Ram sends this message to Sita through Hanuman. She is captive, threatened by Ravana, and has nearly lost hope. Hanuman has just given her Ram's ring and told her the whole story of his search. Sita replies that speaking of pain lightens it a little, but there is no one to tell, and only her own heart knows the truth of the love between her and Ram. The distance you feel now has its own shape, and only you carry it fully.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You are 8000 miles away while your mom lives alone in Indore and had a dizzy spell. Krishna sends a message to his mother Yashoda from far away, saying that since he left her, no one has called him by his pet name. Like him, you may feel unseen in a distant city while missing the warmth of home.
meaning: Krishna is in Mathura, far from his home. He sends a message to his mother Yashoda. He tells her that since he left her, no one there calls him by his pet name Kanhaiya. He also says he has not eaten breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk in the evening. The verse shows that missing home is a form of love. It speaks of a quiet hunger for the care that only a familiar voice can give. You are far from the person who knows your name in the way she used to. The distance makes the missing sharper, not softer.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You miss your mummy papa and worry about their health while studying away from them. Krishna tells his mother Yashoda, 'Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name.' Being far from home can make you feel unseen in your daily routine. You might find a small comfort in holding onto a private name or memory that belongs only to your family.
meaning: Krishna sends a message to his mother Yashoda while he is far from home in Mathura. He tells her that since he left her, no one there calls him by his pet name. He says he has not had his morning breakfast or his evening warm milk since the day he was parted from her. Missing your parents while you study away from them is simply the weight of love.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: Arjuna asks this, and many of us ask it too: what pushes a person to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? If you're carrying something you did, you've probably asked it at night. The Gita treats the question as worth a full answer.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong against their own will, as if pushed by some outside force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger. This anger clouds a person's wisdom the way smoke hides a fire. The verse proposes that a person can master this enemy only by seeing it clearly for what it is. Your parents are gone now, and you are left with the weight of what you think you did wrong. The verse names the force behind that wrong act as desire that turned sour.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You stay awake watching your mother’s breath. Krishna, far from home, tells his mother Yashoda that since he left, no one has called him by his pet name. In your own watching, you too may feel unseen in your care. Let her steady breathing tonight be the quiet name by which you know she is safe.
meaning: Krishna sends a message to his mother Yashoda from Mathura. He tells her that since he left home, no one there calls him by his pet name. He adds that he has gone without his morning food and his evening warm milk. The verse says that missing home is love. You watch your mother breathe through the night. The verse shows that love lives in the small names and habits that only home keeps.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: Dad's surgery is next week in Chennai while you are stuck in the middle of your semester. Krishna, far from home in Mathura, tells his mother Yashoda, "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name." You are in a city where no one knows the name from home, and the distance is real right now. That unnamed absence in your daily life mirrors his, and the verse simply names what it is to be far when someone you love is waiting.
meaning: Krishna is far from his home in Mathura. He sends a message to his mother Yashoda. He tells her that since he left, no one there calls him by his pet name. He says he has not eaten his morning food, and he has not had warm milk in the evening. The verse shows that missing home is a form of love. You are far from your father while he faces surgery, and the unnamed gap in your days is real.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You carry the weight of building a life across the ocean while your parents in Punjab struggle to care for each other. Krishna, far from Mathura, tells his mother Yashoda that since he left her, no one there calls him by his childhood name, Kanhaiya, and he has gone without his morning food or evening milk. Your Sunday calls echo a similar hunger, a name or presence that only home knew, reminding you that distance can silence the everyday tenderness you still long for.
meaning: Krishna sends word to his mother Yashoda from Mathura. He tells her that since he left her home, no one there calls him by his childhood name Kanhaiya. He also notes that he has gone without his morning food and his evening warm milk. The verse shows that missing home is itself a form of love, not a failure of duty. Your Sunday calls carry the same ache, a hunger for the tenderness that only home knew.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: With mummy’s dialysis three times a week and small children to raise, your days carry a heavy weight. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. When your thoughts race tonight, you can notice that same wind without trying to pin it down, and rest your hand on your child’s shoulder as the verse names the storm.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after hearing about discipline of the mind. He admits that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees that the mind is difficult to control, yet he adds that steady practice and letting go can train it over time. Your days already carry the weight of your mother's dialysis and young children, so this restlessness is not a failure on your part.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Your mind feels as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna hears Arjuna say this after admitting his own thoughts are restless, stormy and stubborn. You are far from alone in this; even the greatest warrior found his mind uncontrollable. When you lie awake wondering about your parents, let the verse simply name that storm as real, not your failure.
meaning: Arjuna tells Krishna that his mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees that the mind is difficult to control. He adds that practice and letting go can train it over time. Your first job away from home brings the same restless storm. The worry about your parents is real, but it is not proof that you are failing at holding yourself together.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You placed your papa in a care home and now live with guilt each day. Krishna tells his mother Yashoda, "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name." In the city, far from home, even a prince becomes unknown. Your papa may feel that distance too, yet your care remains real, and his name still belongs to you.
meaning: Krishna sends word to his mother Yashoda from Mathura, where he lives far from home. He tells her that since he left, no one there calls him by his pet name. He says he has missed his morning food and his evening warm milk. The verse says that missing home is love. It means that distance does not erase care, and that being away from those who know you best leaves a quiet ache. Your guilt carries the same weight as Krishna's missing his mother. The distance between you and your papa does not undo the care you still hold for him.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You are far from your mum today, cutting a cake on a screen while she celebrates. Krishna, far from his mother Yashoda, tells her that since he left, no one has called him by his pet name, Kanhaiya. Like him, you may feel unseen in a distant city where no one knows the name you carry at home. Hold that video call a little longer, and let her hear your voice plainly.
meaning: Krishna sends a message from Mathura to his mother Yashoda, who raised him. He tells her to stay well, and says that in four or five days he and his brother will return. He adds that since the day he left her, no one has called him by his pet name, Kanhaiya. He says he has not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk in the evening. You are far from the place where your own name was shaped, and that distance leaves a quiet ache.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: Your mother is in Kolkata with a carer, and you cannot travel easily anymore, so every week you worry. Krishna, far from home in Mathura, tells his mother Yashoda, "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name." Like him, you may feel unseen in this season of distance, yet the name you carry still belongs to those who love you. When the next week of worry comes, let that childhood name remind you of the bond that no distance can erase.
meaning: Krishna sends a message to his mother Yashoda while he is far from home in Mathura. He tells her that since the day he left her, no one has called him by his pet name Kanhaiya. He adds that he has not eaten breakfast in the morning or had warm milk in the evening. He means that missing home is love. The distance has taken away the small daily care of his mother, and that absence is itself a sign of how much he belongs to her.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna calls these mātrā-sparśa: contacts, things that touch you and move on. A deadline, a bad week, a hard meeting. They hurt while they last, they pass, and Krishna asks you to bear them (titikṣasva) until they do.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna has collapsed in grief on the battlefield. He tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These experiences arrive and then leave. They do not stay. He asks Arjuna to bear them with patience.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Your sixteen-year-old son stays on his phone through the night and shuts the door when you try to talk. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. That same restlessness can show up in you now, with thoughts that loop late into the night. When you lie awake, you are holding something as wild as the wind itself.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after hearing about the discipline of the mind. He admits that his thoughts race and resist every attempt to settle them. He compares the effort to grasping the wind. Krishna accepts this difficulty. He then explains that steady practice and the habit of letting go are what gradually train the mind to rest. That same turbulence is moving through you now as you sit with your son's silence and your own late night thoughts.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You move through school runs, swim class, homework, and work calls with no time to breathe as a dad. Bhasa tells his old friend, 'Done this, doing this, must do that'—caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest. Your depths are dancing with worry too. Notice the bird of your mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, fainting between one task and the next.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to Vilasa, his old childhood friend, after they meet again as old men. Vilasa admits he has never found peace. Bhasa tells him that years of hard effort without inner understanding leave a person exactly where they started. The mind is carried along on endless waves of tasks. It never rests. It thinks, this is done, this is happening, this must happen. The bird of the mind grows tangled in a net of reckonings and faints. Your years of hard effort to hold everything together can leave you exactly where you began, with no room to breathe.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You carry the weight of your daughter's silence into every night. Bhasa speaks the mind caught on endless waves of tasks, saying, 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do,' so the bird of the mind faints in its net of reckonings. Tonight, let the list rest; hear the depths still beneath the worry.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to his old friend Vilasa after they meet again as old men. Vilasa asks if he is well, and Bhasa answers that there is no wellness while the mind keeps spinning through endless tasks and worries. He describes a mind carried along on great waves of tasks, never resting for a moment. It keeps tallying what is done, what is being done, and what must be done next. Caught in this net of reckonings, the bird of the mind faints.

verse_text.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse_text.setting: Ashtavakra's 'special instruction' to Janaka on why striving and study do not bring peace.
verse_text.line: Everyone suffers from constant straining, and no one notices. Seeing this alone brings peace.
verse_text.translation: Everyone is miserable from straining after things, and no one realises it. By this single teaching the fortunate one finds peace.

days.reading: Ashtavakra tells Janaka that everyone suffers from constant straining, and no one notices. The text sees this misery coming from the mind's endless ride on effort, even when study or care is involved. Each night, your thoughts circle your daughter's silence, caught in that same unseen strain.

verse_text.speaker: Seer
verse_text.setting: The second birth: raising a child.
verse_text.line: Caring for your child, you care for yourself. Through them you are born a second time.
verse_text.translation: When he cares for the child from birth onward, he is caring for himself, for the continuation of these worlds; that is how they continue. That is his second birth.

days.reading: The Aitareya Upanishad says that when you care for your child from birth onward, you are caring for yourself, and through them you are born a second time. This speaks to your overthinking by grounding you in the fact that nurturing your daughter is already sustaining your own self. Rest in the concrete reality of her care as your own continuation.

verse_text.speaker: Shiva
verse_text.setting: Shiva tells the ancestors that guiding people beats punishing them.
verse_text.line: Better than punishing people is helping them so they never deserve punishment.
verse_text.translation: But the effort by which people never come to deserve punishment at all, made in the company of the wise, is the better one.

days.reading: Shiva tells the ancestors that helping people so they never deserve punishment is better than punishing them. This points to the care you give your daughter each night, building her up gently rather than reacting with force. Let that steady, guiding presence be the ground you stand on today.

verse_text.speaker: Seer
verse_text.setting: The Aitareya on the three births of a person, beginning with pregnancy.
verse_text.line: She who nourishes the child must herself be nourished.
verse_text.translation: It becomes one with the woman, like a part of her own body, so it does not harm her. She nourishes this self of his that has come into her. She who nourishes must herself be nourished. The woman carries the child; the father cares for the child from birth onward.

days.reading: The Aitareya Upanishad says that she who nourishes the child must herself be nourished. After days of endless mental lists, this points to your own body as the first thing to feed. You could set one small plate of food aside for yourself before anyone else eats tonight.

verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: 'The Ideal of a Universal Religion', America, on how anyone grows.
verse_text.line: Your duty is to afford opportunities and to remove obstacles.
verse_text.translation: Do you think you can teach even a child? You cannot. The child teaches himself. Your duty is to afford opportunities and to remove obstacles. A plant grows. Do you make the plant grow? Your duty is to put a hedge round it and see that no animal eats up the plant, and there your duty ends.

days.reading: Swami Vivekananda says your duty is to afford opportunities and remove obstacles, like a gardener who only puts a hedge around a plant so no animal eats it. You could today step back from trying to force your daughter's words and simply clear one small obstacle, such as quieting the room when she tries to speak. The plant grows by itself; your hedge is enough.

story.title: A poor widow's small son is afraid to walk home through the woods
story.summary: Gopala's mother is a widow, very poor, who has toiled at her spinning wheel for months to buy his school things. One winter afternoon he tells her he is afraid to walk home alone through the dark woods; other boys have someone to fetch them. 'Never before had she felt her widowhood, her loneliness, her poverty so bitter.'
story.lesson: A parent's faith, passed to a child, makes the child unafraid; love and faith, more than learning, bring the Lord near.

days.reading: Swami Vivekananda retold a devotional tale of a poor widow whose son fears walking home through dark woods. When her loneliness and poverty feel bitter, she remembers the Lord carries what is needed for those who depend on him, then tells her boy to call his brother Gopala in the trees. Your overthinking at night can meet the same trust: you can tell your daughter that another Gopala tends the woods, and call out to him when darkness feels heavy.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You carry a son's school days like a daily battle, and you feel worn thin. Bhasa tells his friend Vilasa, 'Done this, doing this, must do that'—the mind caught on endless waves of tasks, its depths dancing with worry. Today, your mind may be that bird, tangled in a net of reckonings, fainting under the weight of what is done, being done, and yet to come.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to his old friend Vilasa, two men who grew up together in a forest hermitage and later spent lonely years in hard austerities. They meet again as old men. Vilasa asks if Bhasa is well. Bhasa answers that there is no wellness while the mind keeps spinning through endless tasks and worries. The verse says the mind is carried on great waves of tasks. It never rests. It dances with worry over what has been done, what is being done, and what must still be done. You are caught in the same current, with your son's school days stretching ahead of you each morning.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: With two children and no help, and your husband coming home late, you carry a heavy load. Bhasa speaks plainly: carried along on endless waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest, tangled in a net of reckonings. Today, those ten minutes you never find might be the quiet shore where the mind finally stops its dance.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to his old friend Vilasa after they meet as graybeards in a forest hermitage. Vilasa admits he has found no peace after decades of hard austerities. Bhasa tells him that years of effort without inner understanding leave a person exactly where they began. The mind is carried on endless waves of tasks and worries. It faints because it is caught in a net of reckonings, always thinking about what has been done, what is being done, and what must yet be done. Your days hold the same endless waves, and the mind has no shore to rest on.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You carry the weight of two small children, both jobs, and a nanny who left just when you needed her most. Bhasa tells his old friend Vilasa, 'Done this, doing this, must do that' — the mind caught in endless lists never rests. Your office hours and evenings are caught in that same net of reckonings, where worry dances without a pause. When the nanny quit, the wave of tasks grew; today, the verse simply names the bird of your mind, tangled and fainting under the load.

It keeps running through what it has done, what it is doing, and what it must do next. Caught in this net of reckonings, the bird of the mind faints and finds no rest. You are caught in the same net of reckonings, where office hours and evenings both spin through lists of what is done and what must come next.

When the next hour brings a new fear, you can notice the same net of reckonings pulling at you, and simply rest in one breath without adding the next task.

Your hourly worry about your baby mirrors this tangled bird of the mind, caught in endless reckonings about what comes next.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: By 6pm you are touched out and talked out, with twins and a three year old to care for. Bali says, "Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery." This weariness of the same tasks over and over speaks directly to your days. You might rest your body tonight, yet the loop of the same tasks waits again at dawn.
meaning: Bali speaks this to himself while sitting alone by his window. He has ruled the three worlds for ages. He looks out and sees the same days and nights repeating. The same tasks come again and again. He feels that this endless cycle mocks a thinking person. The verse proposes that the work is not to add more tasks but to master the mind that runs the loop. Your body is tired by evening because the same care repeats. The verse points to the mind that keeps the loop alive, not to more rest alone.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You are raising a teenager while your mind races. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, and that holding it feels like holding the wind. When your thoughts loop through the night, you are facing the same force Arjuna named. You can notice the wind without trying to grip it, and let your attention rest on the breath in your chest.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the field before battle. He admits that his mind refuses to stay still. It is turbulent and hard to control. He compares it to the wind, which cannot be grasped in the hand. Krishna accepts this difficulty. He says that steady practice and the habit of letting go can gradually train the mind. Your mind is racing while you parent a teenager, and that restlessness is not a failure on your part.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Your mind feels as hard to hold as the wind, Krishna says, and you feel consumed by worry while your son sits at home. The Gita names this restlessness as stubborn and strong, not a failure on your part. When the thoughts loop tonight, let that description stand as the wind itself, and rest in the simple fact that your son has been home for two years.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after hearing about the discipline of yoga. He admits that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it seems as hard to control as the wind. Krishna answers that practice and letting go can train this mind. Your worry about your son sitting at home mirrors the restlessness Arjuna names. The text calls this stubborn strength, not a flaw in you.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.
verse_text.line: The mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy.
verse_text.translation: The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy.

reading: You have been planning to start the gym on Monday since January. Rama tells the sages that the mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy. That restlessness might be why the plan keeps flying away before you ever walk through the door.
meaning: Rama speaks to the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha after they ask him to explain his restlessness. He has been watching how the mind behaves. It swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy. The verse names this habit plainly. It offers no fix. It simply asks what is empty inside. Your January plan keeps landing and leaving because the mind is hungry for a start but not for the doing.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.

verse_text.translation: The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy.

verse_text.translation: The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy.

reading: You have been putting off building a website for your business for six months. Rama describes the mind as a bird that pounces on a task like food, then drops it like a bored child's toy. That restlessness can show up today in the gap between knowing what to do and actually opening the work.
meaning: Rama speaks to the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha after they ask him to explain what troubles him. He is a young prince who has seen how wealth hardens people and how time consumes everything. He tells them that the mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy. He is naming a restlessness he cannot yet fix. Your own delay with the website may be this same swooping and dropping, not a lack of will.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You have wanted to write a book for ten years, yet not one chapter exists. Rama's attendant tells King Dasharatha that the prince no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work; he just keeps silent. This quiet withdrawal speaks to your own stillness today, where the work waits and the laughter has faded into silence.
meaning: One of Rama's attendants speaks to King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Sixteen-year-old Rama has come home and stopped eating, stopped laughing, and left his duties. The attendant reports that the boy no longer lights up at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work. He just keeps silent. The verse proposes that this loss of interest is not merely emptiness. It can be the beginning of deeper questioning, provided someone wise helps the person through it. You have carried a book inside you for ten years, and now the page stays blank. This stillness around your work may be the first sign that something in you is ready to ask better questions.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You feel like garbage when your Sunday list stays untouched by Wednesday. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong against their will, as if pushed by force. This verse names that inner push you cannot simply start against, without judging your time or effort.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong against his will, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that it is desire. When a desire is blocked or unmet, it turns into anger. That anger clouds a person's wisdom and judgment. The verse proposes that you can master this force only by seeing it clearly for what it is, not by fighting it with willpower alone. You feel that inner push when your Sunday list stays untouched by Wednesday, and this verse names it as desire turning into anger rather than simple laziness.

Tomorrow, when the phone is in your hand at dawn, notice the pull and let the question sit there.

Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this anger clouds a person's wisdom like smoke hiding a flame. The verse says you can master this force once you see it clearly. That pull toward the screen is a force, not a simple choice you failed to make.

verse_text.speaker: Nidagha
verse_text.setting: Nidagha on craving.
verse_text.line: Every good quality I take up, craving gnaws through, like a mouse chewing a string.
verse_text.translation: Whatever good quality I take refuge in, great sage, craving cuts it away, as a mouse gnaws through a string.

reading: You find that the latest purchase already feels old. Nidagha tells Ribhu that whatever good quality he takes up, craving gnaws through it like a mouse chewing a string. That restless pull toward the next thing can silently cut through what you just gained. Notice how the string frays even when you hold it steady.
meaning: Nidagha speaks to his teacher Ribhu after returning from a long pilgrimage. He is heavy with disappointment. He tells Ribhu that no matter what good quality he takes up, craving cuts it away. It works like a mouse gnawing through a string. The verse names a restless mind that cannot settle on what it has. You felt that pull the moment the last purchase turned familiar. The verse names that same hunger before it asks you to do anything about it.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You feel controlled by sale notifications while your closet stays full of tagged things. Arjuna tells Krishna his nature is stricken by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right, so he asks to be taught plainly what is best. Today, you can lay one tagged item down and simply ask what clarity looks like for you, without buying another.
meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield and tells Krishna that his nature is stricken by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right. He asks Krishna to tell him for certain what is best. He presents himself as a student who has come to learn. You are asking for clarity because the pull of sale notifications has left you unsure of what you actually want.
