The flat savings and the endless planning may come from that same gnawing, not from a lack of income.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.
verse_text.line: The moth doesn't know the flame burns. We know, and still we don't let go.
verse_text.translation: Let the moth fall into the blazing flame not knowing that it burns; let the fish swallow the bait not knowing the hook. But we, knowing full well, still do not let go of desires tangled in a net of dangers. Ah, how deep is the power of delusion!

meaning: Bhartrihari speaks from his own turning away from the world. He addresses anyone still caught in wanting. He points to the moth and the fish. The moth flies into the flame and does not know it burns. The fish takes the bait and does not know the hook waits. We are not like them. We see the danger clearly. Yet we still hold on to desires that trap us. He asks us to release them before they drag us down, and to stop calling forced relief a kind of happiness. The restlessness you carry is the net tightening around a want you still name as security.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.
verse_text.line: The moth doesn't know the flame burns. We know, and still we don't let go.
verse_text.translation: Let the moth fall into the blazing flame not knowing that it burns; let the fish swallow the bait not knowing the hook. But we, knowing full well, still do not let go of desires tangled in a net of dangers. Ah, how deep is the power of delusion!

reading: You find yourself unable to stop when something sweet appears, swearing anew each day yet breaking the vow again. Bhartrihari asks how the moth can fall into the blazing flame not knowing it burns, or the fish swallow bait unaware of the hook. You know the cost, yet still you do not let go of what tangles you. Today, when that next craving rises, notice the flame before your hand reaches for it.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines from The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures to anyone who reads them. He sets up two creatures that act without knowledge. A moth flies into a blazing flame and does not know it burns. A fish swallows bait and does not feel the hidden hook. Then he turns to people. We know full well that desires are tangled in a net of dangers. Still we do not let go. He asks how deep the power of delusion can be. You know the cost of reaching for something sweet, yet the pull returns before the day ends.

verse_text.speaker: Indra, disguised as a jackal
verse_text.setting: The jackal tells Kashyapa that getting more will not cure his discontent.
verse_text.line: Getting what you want doesn't satisfy. Craving grows like a fire fed with more wood.
verse_text.translation: There is no satisfaction in getting what you want. Craving is not put out by water; it only blazes up more, like a fire fed with fuel.

days.reading: Bhishma, speaking as a jackal to Kashyapa, says that getting what you want brings no satisfaction, and craving only blazes up more like a fire fed with fuel. You notice this pattern when sweet things catch your eye and break a daily vow. The verse sees the source in the act of feeding the flame, not in any lack within you.

verse_text.speaker: Yama
verse_text.setting: Nachiketa has refused wealth and long life; Yama begins teaching.
verse_text.line: The good and the pleasant both knock. The wise choose the good; the foolish grab the pleasant.
verse_text.translation: The good and the pleasant both come to a person. The wise one examines them and tells them apart. The wise chooses the good over the pleasant; the dull chooses the pleasant, for getting and keeping.

days.reading: Yama tells Nachiketa that the good and the pleasant both come to a person, and the wise examine them to tell them apart, choosing the good over the pleasant. You feel restless as sweet things pull you in daily, yet you keep breaking your own daily vow. Stand on the ground of separating what truly serves you from what merely tastes good right now.

verse_text.speaker: Manki
verse_text.setting: Manki, after his last savings are lost in a freak accident, speaks to his own desire.
verse_text.line: Desire, I know your root: my own imagining. I'll stop feeding you, and you'll be gone.
verse_text.translation: Desire, I know your root: you are born of my own imagining. I will not imagine you any more, and you will be gone, root and all.

days.reading: Bhishma, speaking as Manki, tells Desire directly: 'I know your root: you are born of my own imagining. I will not imagine you any more, and you will be gone.' After losing everything, Manki stops feeding the craving with mental pictures. You, too, can pause the imagining that drives your restlessness, and let the urge lose its ground.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Like a tortoise pulling in its limbs, draw your senses back from what pulls at them.
verse_text.translation: When, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs on every side, a person withdraws the senses from their objects, his wisdom is firmly set.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that a steady mind pulls its senses back like a tortoise drawing in its limbs. You could try pulling your gaze away the moment something sweet appears, letting your eyes rest instead of reaching for it. This small pause mirrors yesterday's choice between the pleasant and the good.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
verse_text.line: When your mind drifts to harmful things, steer it back to good ones. That's the whole teaching.
verse_text.translation: When the mind has sunk into bad things, bring it down into good ones with effort. That is the summary of all the scriptures.

days.reading: Vasishtha tells Rama that when the mind sinks into harmful things, you could steer it back to good ones with effort. This echoes your daily cycle of craving sweets and breaking your own vows. The teaching is simply to redirect the drifting mind toward what steadies it.

story.title: Manki's song: desire, I know your root
story.summary: Manki spends all he has on a pair of oxen; both are killed in an accident. In his despair he sees through desire: it is born of his own imagining, and he resolves to forgive insults and stop feeding it. Bhishma adds Janaka's verse on owning nothing.
story.lesson: Desire grows from what we imagine. Stop feeding it, and it fades.

days.reading: Manki watches his last money vanish when a camel bolts with his two young bulls dangling from its neck, and he first blames fate before turning to desire itself. You keep promising yourself you will stop reaching for the next sweet thing, yet the pull returns. Manki names his own imagining as the root and refuses to feed it; today you can notice the moment you stop imagining that next fix, and watch what actually remains.

verse_text.speaker: Nidagha
verse_text.setting: Nidagha on craving.
verse_text.line: Every good quality I take up, craving gnaws through, like a mouse chewing a string.
verse_text.translation: Whatever good quality I take refuge in, great sage, craving cuts it away, as a mouse gnaws through a string.

reading: You carry a restlessness that always wants more. Nidagha tells Ribhu that whatever good quality he takes up, craving gnaws through it like a mouse chewing a string. Your next thing might feel like relief, yet the wanting keeps cutting. Notice where the string frays today.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You order things every week yet still feel empty. Young Rama asks, "What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?" Your home fills up, but the question remains: whose is all this, and what has anyone gained? Let the things arrive and stay, while you sit with Rama's question about what actually belongs to you.
meaning: Young Rama has just returned from his travels and sits in his father's court. The sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha are there with him. Rama tells them that nothing interests him anymore. He asks what kingship means to him and what pleasures are worth having. He wonders who he really is and what all this is for. If the world is unreal, let it be unreal. He asks whose it truly is and what anyone has actually gained. The verse is a plain question about emptiness, not a solution. You order things every week yet still feel empty. Young Rama asks what kingship means to him and what anyone has gained. Your home fills up, but the question stays open about what actually belongs to you.

verse_text.speaker: Nidagha
verse_text.setting: Nidagha on craving.
verse_text.line: Every good quality I take up, craving gnaws through, like a mouse chewing a string.
verse_text.translation: Whatever good quality I take refuge in, great sage, craving cuts it away, as a mouse gnaws through a string.

reading: You described gaming till 4am on weeknights, always chasing one more match. Nidagha speaks of craving gnawing through every good quality like a mouse chewing a string. Your guilt may sit beside that same endless wanting, yet the verse simply names how craving cuts away what you try to hold. When the next match calls tonight, you might notice the string fraying, and choose to lay the controller down.
meaning: Young Nidagha comes back from a long pilgrimage. He is tired and disappointed. He speaks to his teacher Ribhu, the wise one. He says that no matter what good quality he picks up, craving eats it away. It is like a mouse chewing through a string. The verse simply names this restlessness. It shows that craving cuts through whatever a person tries to hold. Your guilt sits beside that same endless wanting. The verse names how craving cuts away what you try to hold.

verse_text.speaker: Vibhishan
verse_text.setting: Vibhishan, Ravana's good-hearted brother, describes his life in Ravana's court.
verse_text.line: I live here like the tongue among the teeth.
verse_text.translation: Son of the wind, hear how I live: like the poor tongue among the teeth. Friend, knowing me to be without support, will the Lord of the Sun dynasty ever show me grace?

reading: It sounds like home doesn't feel safe right now.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You have a good salary, a nice flat, and a healthy family, yet inside it all feels flat, and you wonder if this is it. Young Rama asks, what is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for? If everything you have built feels unreal, let it be unreal for now; you can simply sit with that question of who you are, without needing an answer today.
meaning: Young Rama returns from his travels and sits in his father's court. The sages there ask him to speak. He tells them that a kingdom means nothing to him, and pleasures mean nothing. He asks who he is, and what all this is for. He says if it is unreal, let it be unreal. He wants to know whose it is, and what anyone has gained. He is naming his emptiness out loud. The verse proposes that saying this out loud is the first step. You have built a good salary, a nice flat, and a healthy family, yet inside it all feels flat. Rama names that same flatness without rushing to fix it.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: The narrator Sanjaya speaks these words. He describes the greatest archer of his time putting down his bow and sitting in the chariot, his mind sunk in sorrow. The Gita begins with someone who can't go on, and it stays with him for seventeen more chapters.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You wonder about your studies, a job, marriage, and children, and feel you cannot understand what it all means. Young Rama asks, 'What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?' His question meets the same quiet confusion you carry today, where the path ahead feels hollow.
meaning: Young Rama returns to his father's court after travels. He tells the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha that nothing interests him. He asks what kingship and pleasure mean to him. He asks who he is and what all this is for. He says if these things are unreal, let them be unreal. He asks whose they are and what anyone has gained. Your studies, a job, marriage and children feel like a track with no finish line. Rama names that same hollow feeling without rushing to fix it.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You said the days blur together and nothing feels meaningful anymore. Rama's attendant tells King Dasharatha that the prince no longer lights up at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work; he just keeps silent. In your raising of kids, that quiet stillness can meet the emptiness you carry today, right in the middle of the blur.
meaning: Rama's attendant speaks to King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Rama has stopped eating properly and sits alone. The attendant reports that Rama no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just keeps silent. The verse presents this quiet withdrawal as the beginning of deeper questioning, provided someone helps the person through it. Your days blur together and nothing feels meaningful anymore. That quiet stillness in Rama meets the emptiness you carry while raising your children.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: After two decades abroad earning for others and building a house back home, you sit in your room wondering what you actually lived for. Young Rama asks, What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for? Your life of doing everything right can meet this same question, opening the space to ask who you are beneath the empty box.
meaning: Young Rama has just returned from his travels. He sits in his father's court before the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha. He tells them that nothing interests him anymore. He asks what kingship or pleasure mean to him. He asks who he is and what all this is for. He says if it is unreal, let it be unreal. He asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. The verse names a moment of honest emptiness. It is a question, not an answer. After two decades of earning and building for others, your life of doing everything right can meet this same question. It opens space to ask who you are beneath the empty box.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You asked why you are doing all this every single day. Bali says, "Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery." Your daily grind can feel exactly like that endless loop, and naming it as mockery is valid. Today, you might let that weariness sit with you without rushing to fix it, simply as the reality of another repeated day.
meaning: Bali speaks this to himself. He is a demon king who has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day he sits by his window and sees the same days and nights pass. He feels that the endless chain of tasks mocks a thinking person. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it. You are asking why you keep doing this every single day. Bali names that same weariness as mockery, and your doubt is valid.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You used to love music and football, and now nothing really lands. The verse says the mind is carried along on endless waves of tasks, never getting a moment's rest, tangled in a net of reckonings. Today, that numbness may be the mind's way of signaling it is caught in too many waves at once. When you pick up a football, let it simply be a ball in your hands, not another task to complete.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to Vilasa, an old friend they meet again after years apart. Vilasa admits he never found peace. Bhasa tells him that years of hard effort without inner understanding leave a person exactly where they started. The mind is carried on endless waves of tasks. It never rests. It dances with worry. It thinks about what was done, what is being done, and what must be done next. Caught in this net of reckonings, the mind faints. That numbness you feel is the mind caught in too many waves at once, unable to land anywhere.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You feel an existential emptiness even while raising kids and working. Rama's attendant tells King Dasharatha that the prince no longer lights up at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work, but simply keeps silent. That quiet stillness speaks to your today: it names the space where nothing feels like it matters, without asking you to fill it.
meaning: In the Yoga Vasishtha, Rama's attendant speaks to King Dasharatha. The king is worried because his son Rama has come home from a long pilgrimage and withdrawn. The attendant reports that the prince no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just keeps silent. The verse proposes that losing interest in everything can be the start of asking better questions, if someone helps you through it. Your emptiness names a space where nothing feels like it matters, even while you raise your children and hold down a job. It does not ask you to fix the feeling right now.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You spent a lifetime running, and now that you have stopped, nothing makes sense. The Yoga Vasishtha records Rama losing interest in jokes, pleasures, and work, falling into silence. Your stillness now echoes that quiet withdrawal, not as an ending, but as a space where the old chase has finally ceased.
meaning: Rama's attendant speaks to King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Rama has stopped eating properly, stopped laughing, and ignores his duties. He sits alone and keeps silent. The attendant reports that Rama no longer lights up at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet. Your lifelong running has finally stopped, and the silence now holds no familiar shape.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You feel spiritually empty, and promotions no longer move you. Bali speaks from his window, saying day and night bring the same tasks again and again, and to a thinking person this feels like a mockery. When your work has become a loop you no longer believe in, this verse names the weariness you carry without asking you to step away from what is yours today.
meaning: Bali speaks to himself from his window after ruling the three worlds for ages. He sees that day follows night and the same tasks return without end. To a thinking person this repetition feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that the work itself is not the trap. The trap is the mind that runs the loop. Mastery comes not from changing the tasks but from mastering the mind that repeats them. You have reached a point where the next title means nothing, because the loop itself has lost its weight.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You wonder why anything matters if we will all be forgotten. Rama's attendant tells King Dasharatha that the prince no longer lights up at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work; he simply keeps silent. In your studying, this quiet withdrawal might be the same stillness, where nothing pulls you forward and you just stop.
meaning: Rama's attendant speaks to the worried King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Sixteen-year-old Rama has withdrawn from his court and his duties. He no longer laughs at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work. He simply keeps silent. The attendant reports this stillness to the king so that others may notice it and help the boy through it. Your studying has gone quiet too. This stillness is not emptiness. It can be the first sign that you are ready to ask harder questions about what matters.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You are searching for meaning and nothing feels like it matters. Young Rama asks, "What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me?" Today, your own work and achievements can hold the same question. You might sit with the fact that the kingdom you built still leaves you asking who you are beneath it.
meaning: Young Rama sits in his father's court after returning from his travels. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha are there with him. He tells them that nothing interests him anymore. He asks what kingship and pleasure mean to him. He asks who he is and what all this is for. He says if it is unreal, let it be unreal. He asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. The verse names a hollow feeling honestly. It is a question and not an answer. You built your own work and it still leaves you asking who you are beneath it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: You joined a top consulting firm and every day you wait for someone to realise they made a mistake hiring you. Krishna tells Arjuna your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. This means the daily doubt about your place belongs to the outcome, which was never yours to control, while your action right here remains intact.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on a battlefield, just before the great war begins. Arjuna is frozen by doubt and grief. He fears that fighting will destroy his family and bring shame. Krishna tells him that a person has a right only to the action itself, never to the fruits that follow. The work belongs to the one who acts. The outcome belongs to forces beyond any single hand. Krishna asks Arjuna to keep doing what is right without clinging to success or failure. The doubt about your place in the firm belongs to the outcome, which was never yours to control. Your action right here remains intact.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You are leading a team for the first time and feel every choice is second-guessed. Arjuna, the finest archer of his age, tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, and that holding it feels like holding the wind. Your looping thoughts echo that same wind, yet the verse names the turbulence without calling it your fault. Let the image of the wind remind you that the mind moves on its own, and rest in the simple fact of your next decision.
meaning: Arjuna, the finest archer of his age, speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He admits that his mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees that the mind is difficult to control, but he adds that steady practice and letting go can train it over time. Your second-guessing is not a sign that you do not belong in the role. It is simply the mind moving like wind, and the verse names that turbulence without calling it your fault.

verse_text.speaker: Sutikshna
verse_text.setting: The young sage Sutikshna hears Ram is coming and runs to meet him, full of doubt about himself.
verse_text.line: I have no devotion, no wisdom, no steady love. But he loves the one who has nowhere else to go.
verse_text.translation: 'Will Ram, my master, with his brother, meet me as he would his own servant? There is no firm trust in my heart; no devotion, detachment or wisdom in my mind; no good company, no yoga, chanting or sacrifice, no steady love for his lotus feet. But the ocean of compassion has one habit: the one who has no other refuge is dear to him.'

reading: You feel uneasy speaking before big clients because your English feels incomplete. Sutikshna says he has no wisdom or steady love, yet the compassionate one loves the person who has nowhere else to go. Your hesitation in that room can simply be where you stand, with no other refuge, and still be met.
meaning: Sutikshna is a young sage. He hears that Ram is coming near his forest home. He runs out to meet him. He is full of doubt about himself. He thinks he has no devotion, no wisdom, no steady love, no chanting, no sacrifice. He still trusts that Ram loves the one who has nowhere else to go.

verse_text.speaker: Sutikshna
verse_text.setting: The young sage Sutikshna hears Ram is coming and runs to meet him, full of doubt about himself.
verse_text.line: I have no devotion, no wisdom, no steady love. But he loves the one who has nowhere else to go.
verse_text.translation: 'Will Ram, my master, with his brother, meet me as he would his own servant? There is no firm trust in my heart; no devotion, detachment or wisdom in my mind; no good company, no yoga, chanting or sacrifice, no steady love for his lotus feet. But the ocean of compassion has one habit: the one who has no other refuge is dear to him.'

reading: You feel you have not earned a raise yet. Sutikshna says he has no devotion, wisdom, or steady love, yet the compassionate one loves the one who has nowhere else to go. Your hesitation before asking for what you want echoes his doubt, but the verse points to a refuge that does not wait for you to be fully ready. Today, you can simply stand in that place of having nowhere else to go.

verse_text.speaker: Sutikshna
verse_text.setting: The young sage Sutikshna hears Ram is coming and runs to meet him, full of doubt about himself.
verse_text.line: I have no devotion, no wisdom, no steady love. But he loves the one who has nowhere else to go.
verse_text.translation: 'Will Ram, my master, with his brother, meet me as he would his own servant? There is no firm trust in my heart; no devotion, detachment or wisdom in my mind; no good company, no yoga, chanting or sacrifice, no steady love for his lotus feet. But the ocean of compassion has one habit: the one who has no other refuge is dear to him.'

reading: You feel sure you will be wrong when your idea is right in the meeting. Sutikshna says he has no wisdom or steady love, yet the one who has nowhere else to go is dear to him. When your mouth stays shut, remember that your refuge is already held, not because you earned it, but because there is nowhere else for you to go.
meaning: Sutikshna is a young sage. He hears that Ram is coming near his hut. He runs out to meet him. He is full of doubt about himself. He thinks he has no devotion, no wisdom, no steady love. He feels he is not worthy. Still he trusts that Ram loves the one who has nowhere else to go. That is the whole point. He does not need to earn this love by being perfect first. You do not have to feel qualified to speak. Your idea can be right even when your mouth stays shut.

verse_text.speaker: Narada
verse_text.setting: Narada, master of every science, comes to Sanatkumara.
verse_text.line: I have learned so much, yet I am sad. I know words, not myself. Help me cross this sorrow.
verse_text.translation: 'Sir, I know only the texts; I do not know the self. I have heard from people like you that one who knows the self crosses beyond sorrow. I am in sorrow, sir. Please take me across.' He said to him: 'Whatever you have studied is only name.'

reading: You feel you are not good at anything. Narada tells Sanatkumara that despite mastering every science, he remains sad because he knows texts but not himself. Today, this points to a gap between what you have done and who you are. Your work may hold many names and skills, yet the verse suggests the sorrow you feel belongs to what is still unknown about yourself, not to a lack in you.
meaning: Narada comes to Sanatkumara, a teacher who knows the infinite. Narada has mastered every science of his time, yet he tells Sanatkumara that he is sad. He admits he knows only texts and words, not himself. Sanatkumara replies that everything Narada has studied is only a name. The verse proposes that learning and success do not end sorrow. Only knowing the infinite, which is beyond all names, crosses beyond sorrow. You have built a life of skills and titles, yet the gap between what you have done and who you are still aches.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. When you take a client call, the outcome of whether they see through you belongs to the result, not to your control. Let the call happen as your action, and set down the fear of being caught before it starts.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is shaken and unsure whether to fight. Krishna tells him that a person has a right only to the action itself, never to its fruits. The outcome belongs to a larger order. One should do the work fully and not let the result become the motive for acting, while also refusing to shrink back into inaction.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

reading: You feel useless now that your work has moved to computers, and you fear looking foolish if you ask. Manu speaks to Vishnu, saying that even when standing before the wish-fulfilling tree, a poor man hesitates to ask, not knowing its power, and doubt rises in his heart. Today, your hesitation before new technology mirrors that ancient doubt, yet the tree is still there, waiting for your request.
meaning: Manu speaks to Vishnu after years of austerity. Vishnu offers him any boon. Manu hesitates, comparing himself to a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree yet still holds back, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in his heart. He finally asks for a son like God himself. Your hesitation before new tools mirrors that ancient doubt, yet the tree is still there, waiting for your request.

verse_text.setting: The young sage Sutikshna hears Ram is coming and runs to meet him, full of doubt about himself.

meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after hearing how to steady the self through discipline. He admits that the mind refuses to stay put. It rushes and resists like air that cannot be grasped. Krishna agrees that the mind is restless and hard to hold. Yet he points to repeated practice and release as the way to train it over time. Your overthinking right now is not a failure of will. It is simply the mind doing what Arjuna named, and it can be met with patience rather than force.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You feel empty inside, and the work around you no longer holds you. Rama's attendant tells King Dasharatha that the prince no longer lights up at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work, but simply keeps silent. In your days now, this quiet withdrawal can be a space where the noise of achievement fades, and you rest in the stillness without forcing anything to matter.
meaning: Rama's attendant speaks to King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Rama is sixteen and has withdrawn into silence. He no longer laughs at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work. The attendant reports that the prince simply keeps silent. The verse proposes that this loss of interest is not mere illness or weakness. It can be the first stirring of deeper questions, provided someone wise helps the person through it. Your work no longer holds you, and the emptiness you feel mirrors Rama's quiet withdrawal after his return.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what becomes of someone who tries and fails; Krishna reassures him.
verse_text.line: What happens to someone who believes, tries, slips, and doesn't make it to the end?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: One who has faith but does not strive enough, whose mind falls away from yoga before reaching perfection, what end does he come to, Krishna?

reading: You feel stuck and unable to get started. Krishna hears Arjuna ask what becomes of someone who believes, tries, slips, and does not make it to the end. This speaks to you today as a reminder that the path itself is witnessed, even when momentum fades. You can return to the very next step without needing to finish everything at once.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna what happens to a person who has faith but does not strive enough, and whose mind falls away from yoga before reaching perfection. Krishna reassures him that no sincere effort is wasted. The person picks up exactly where they left off, and their past effort carries forward into the next attempt.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You carry guilt as a parent. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong against his will, as if pushed by force. This verse names the struggle you feel today: the gap between what you want to do and what you end up doing. Let that question sit with you as you face tomorrow morning.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against his own will, as if pushed by some force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this anger is the enemy that clouds a person's wisdom. He tells Arjuna to see this clearly and master it.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: Ram speaks to Kaikeyi after accepting exile, yet one sorrow still burns his heart: his father did not tell him himself about the coronation. You carry a similar ache today from someone close who left you wounded. That silence from a person near to you can sting more than the event itself. You might still give them everything unasked, even now.
meaning: Ram speaks to Kaikeyi after he has accepted fourteen years in the forest. He agrees to leave without anger. Yet one sorrow still burns his heart. The king did not tell him himself about Bharata's coronation. The pain is not the exile. It is the silence of the one who should have spoken first. Someone near to you delivered a hard truth without facing you directly. That silence can sting more than the news itself.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You carry a hurt that still burns. Ram says the exile itself did not wound him most; what stung was that his father did not tell him the news himself. That silence from someone close can leave a sharper ache than any loud wrong. Today, you might let that unspoken distance simply be what it is, without trying to explain it away.
meaning: Ram speaks these words to Kaikeyi after he has accepted fourteen years of exile in the forest. He has agreed to leave without anger. Yet one thing still burns in him. He tells her that the exile itself did not wound him most. What stung was that his father did not tell him the news himself. The hurt comes from a silence where a word was expected.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You feel lost right now. Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed by grief to go on. Like Arjuna letting his weapons fall, you too can set down the weight you are carrying today and simply sit, without forcing yourself forward.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra from the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid down his bow and arrows and collapsed onto his seat. He is too overwhelmed by grief to continue. The verse records that even a mighty warrior can freeze when the cost of action becomes unbearable. You are in that same frozen moment. The weight you carry has stopped you in your tracks, and that stillness is real.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: Feeling alone at this working stage, you carry a quiet ache. Krishna tells Arjuna that one who sees him everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him, nor he to Krishna. This means the distance you feel does not erase a presence that remains fixed upon you. You can notice one ordinary thing today and let it stand as proof that you are still held.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has asked how a person can keep the mind steady while living in the world. Krishna answers that the one who sees him in every being and sees every being within him will never be separated from him. The idea is that a settled mind comes from moderation and from gently bringing the attention back again and again. The distance you feel at work does not remove a presence that stays fixed upon you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: Feeling lonely while studying is hard. Krishna tells Arjuna to see him in everything and everything in him, adding that he never loses him, nor he him. When you look around your campus and notice the same presence in the people and places there, you might find that connection is already closer than you feel right now.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna while teaching him how to settle his mind in meditation. He tells Arjuna that a person who sees him in all things and sees all things within him will never be separated from him. The verse proposes that steady attention and returning gently to that view again and again is what calms the mind. You are far from home and the quiet feels heavy right now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You carry a peaceful feeling right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that the one whose happiness, delight and light are entirely within becomes one with Brahman and reaches lasting freedom. This speaks to you today by pointing to the quiet steadiness already within your work life, a light that does not depend on outside turns.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has asked about the one who knows, and Krishna describes the wise person. He says this person finds happiness inside themselves, finds delight inside themselves, and finds light inside themselves. That yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman. The verse proposes that lasting freedom comes from an inner source, not from pleasures that begin and end. You already carry a peaceful feeling in your work life. The verse points to the quiet steadiness inside you, a light that does not depend on outside turns.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: You feel inspired right now as you run your own thing. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one people follow. Your next step can simply be the steady way you keep showing up, letting that grounded presence become the quiet example others naturally notice.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the field before battle. Arjuna has been asking why someone who already knows the truth still acts. Krishna answers that even the fulfilled keep working. The wise do not act for their own gain. They act because the world watches them. Whatever a respected person does, others copy. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows. You are running your own thing and you feel inspired. That pull to keep going comes from knowing your presence matters beyond your own results.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: You feel inspired right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is what the world follows. Your grounded actions today can quietly shape the space around your studies, becoming the steady example others naturally notice.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while they stand on the field before battle. Arjuna has asked why a person who has found everything should still act. Krishna answers that even those who are fully content keep working. They do it because people watch what they do. They follow the standard that person sets. The verse says people copy actions, not words. Your inspiration right now can become a quiet standard for those around your studies. Your grounded actions today shape the space you share without a word spoken.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel grateful. Bhartrihari asks what generous austerity earned this freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, good company, and learning that brings calm. Your mind stirring gently even as it looks outward mirrors that quiet grace. Notice the simple nourishment before you today, and let that be enough.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his Worship of Shiva. He is an ascetic poet looking back on his life. He names four gifts. Freedom to wander without chains. Food that does not come with shame. Noble company. Learning that only brings calm. He wonders what hard practice earned such a gentle mind. The verse proposes that a simple life is a rare fruit. It asks for gratitude rather than rivalry between forms of God. You carry a sense of thanks for the steadiness you have built. The verse names the quiet gifts that make that steadiness possible.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You feel hopeful about what lies ahead now that you are retired. Lakshmana tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful and that for the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. This suggests that the energy you already feel can carry you into fresh beginnings without forcing any particular path.
meaning: Lakshman speaks to Ram at Lake Pampa after Sita has been taken. Spring surrounds them, and the beauty of the place only sharpens Ram's grief. Lakshman tells him that enthusiasm holds the greatest strength. For the person who carries it, nothing in the world remains out of reach. The hope you feel now can carry you into what comes next without forcing a single path ahead.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You feel a strong resolve right now. Savitri tells her father-in-law that she began this with determination, and that same determination will carry her to the end. That same steady force can carry your own resolve through to its finish today.
meaning: Savitri speaks to Dyumatsena, her father-in-law, after she learns that her husband Satyavan will die in three days. She has begun a hard three night vow. Dyumatsena is worried for her. Savitri tells him not to be distressed. She says she began this with determination, and that same determination will carry her to the end. She means that a firm will begun at the start is what sees a hard task through to its close. You began something hard and you mean to finish it. That same force can carry your own resolve through to its close today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among those welcomed to turn toward the divine. Let this open door stand with you as you sit with the text today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He explains that four kinds of good people come to him in worship. These are the distressed, the curious, those who seek wealth, and the wise. He makes clear that any reason brings a person to the divine. No motive is turned away. Your curiosity is one of the four doors Krishna names. It is enough to bring you to this text today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people turn to the divine: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among them. It is a valid way to approach what lies beyond the everyday, right where you are in your working life.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is caught between two armies and does not yet understand why he is there. Krishna explains that four kinds of people turn toward the divine. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. Each comes from a different place, but all are welcome. Your curiosity is not a distraction from your working life. It is one of the four ways people reach toward what lies beyond the everyday.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain, which come and go and do not last. You carry a feeling of anxiousness while raising kids. This verse invites you to notice that what moves through you is temporary, like weather passing through a room. Let your next breath rest in that passing, without trying to fix what is already shifting.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna grieves the coming war. He tells him that the self never begins and never ends. Bodies change like clothes. Sensible things touch the senses and bring cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings arrive and depart. They do not remain. Arjuna is asked to bear them with patience while he learns what truly endures beyond every loss. You carry anxiousness while raising your children. This invites you to notice that what moves through you now is temporary, like weather passing through a room.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel anxious while caring for your parents. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and their objects brings heat and cold, pleasure and pain, which come and go and do not last, so one should bear them patiently. In your days of caregiving, this means the shifting weight of worry and duty passes like weather, and you can meet each moment as it arrives, letting the anxious sensation come and go without clinging to it.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield of after Arjuna lays down his weapons in grief. Arjuna has just said that killing his own kin would bring sin and destroy the family order. Krishna answers by teaching that the true self within every person is never born and never dies. The contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These sensations arrive and depart like passing clouds. They do not last. A person should bear them with patience instead of letting them overturn the mind. In your days of caregiving, the shifting weight of worry and duty passes like weather. You can meet each moment as it arrives, letting the anxious sensation come and go without clinging to it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain, which come and go and do not last. You are feeling anxious now, and this verse invites you to notice how these shifting sensations pass through you like weather. Rest your attention on one steady breath today, feeling the air move without trying to change it.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that the contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These experiences come and go. They do not last. Arjuna must learn to bear them with patience. The true self within never dies and never comes into being. The anxiousness you carry now is a passing sensation, not the whole of who you are. It will move through you like weather and leave.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You carry a restless feeling while running your own thing. Bhasa tells Vilasa that the mind, caught on endless waves of tasks—'done this, doing this, must do that'—faints in a net of reckonings and finds no rest. Today, that same loop might be circling around you. Notice one unfinished task on your desk, and let your breath rest there for a moment.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to Vilasa, an old friend they have not seen since childhood. They meet again as old men after years of lonely hard effort. Vilasa admits he has never found peace. Bhasa tells him that being carried along on endless great waves of tasks means the mind never rests. Its depths dance with worry. The mind repeats what it has done, what it is doing, and what it must do next. Caught in a net of reckonings, the bird of the mind faints. Your own work has become a loop of endless lists. The verse names that loop without blaming you for it.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

reading: You feel uneasy about whether you are good enough at work. Manu says that even before the wishing tree, a poor man hesitates to ask for what he truly wants, not knowing its power. Today, your doubt may be hiding the strength you already stand near. Let your next step be simply naming one thing you actually want.
meaning: King Manu and Queen Shatarupa realise in old age that a whole life has passed without what mattered most. They hand over the kingdom and practise austerity for years. When Vishnu offers a boon, Manu hesitates like a poor man before the wish-fulfilling tree, then asks for a son like God himself. You are at the start of your work life and that unease is sitting with you now.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You feel overthinking right now. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and that holding it feels like holding the wind. Your thoughts today carry that same force. When the mind races, you can simply notice its movement without trying to pin it down, like feeling the breeze pass.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the field before battle. He admits that his mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees that the mind is difficult to control, yet practice and letting go can gradually train it. Your thoughts carry that same force right now, and trying to pin them down only exhausts you.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You feel empty now that your active years have passed. Young Rama asks what kingship or pleasure means to him, and who he truly is amid it all. This same questioning can sit with you as you let go of what once defined your days, resting in the simple fact that nothing here needs to be real to be set down.
meaning: Young Rama has just returned from his travels. He sits in his father's court before the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha. He tells them he finds no interest in anything around him. He asks what kingship means to him, and what pleasures are worth having. He asks who he truly is, and what all this is for. He says if the world is unreal, let it be unreal. He asks whose it really is, and what anyone has gained. He is naming the emptiness he feels. He is not giving the answer yet. You feel this same hollow space now that your active years have passed. The question can sit with you as you let go of what once defined your days.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from that comes desire, and from desire, anger. You feel anger right now. The verse names a path from dwelling to attachment to blocked wanting. Notice where your mind has settled today, and let that awareness sit with you.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna what a person of steady mind looks like in speech, posture and walk. Krishna describes someone content within and unshaken by sorrow. Then he traces a chain. When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire. From desire comes anger when it is blocked. The verse proposes that steadiness is built by guarding where attention settles. You are raising children and anger is sitting heavy in you right now. The verse points to the path your mind may have taken today, from a settled thought to a blocked wanting.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You feel empty right now. Young Rama asks in his father's court, 'What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?' His words echo your own drifting between paths. You can let the unreal feel unreal, and simply sit with the question of who you are today.
meaning: Young Rama stands in his father's court after returning from his travels. The sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask him to speak. He tells them that wealth hardens people, time eats everything, and the mind never fills. He asks what kingship and pleasure mean to him, who he is, and what all this is for. He says only the company of good people gives him hope. Your drifting between paths carries the same honest weight. You do not have to name the answer yet.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You are anxious while working through a visa documents checklist for a UK visitor visa. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, and that holding it feels like holding the wind. Your thoughts may race across that same checklist right now; the verse simply names the wind-like mind, and you can set the papers down beside it, even for a moment.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after admitting his own confusion. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He compares trying to control it to grasping the wind. Krishna agrees that the mind is hard to hold. He adds that steady practice and letting go can gradually train it. Your mind is racing across that visa checklist right now. The verse names that restlessness without judging it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that people turn toward the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom, and all four kinds are welcome. Your curiosity places you among those who seek knowledge. Let this verse meet you today as you open the Gita, simply as one of these four who is already welcome.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He is explaining why people miss the divine and who instead turns to it. He tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him. These are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. Your curiosity already places you among those who seek knowledge. You do not need to wait until you feel certain before you belong here.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel restless. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact with the senses brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and they come and go. You can bear the deadlines and demands pressing on you today without letting them settle as your whole state.

story.title: Pingala's song
story.summary: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira about Pingala, who sat awake one night waiting for a lover who never came. Every sound outside might have been his footsteps, so she kept listening. Late in the night she saw what was keeping her awake. It was her hope that someone else would arrive and settle her. She let that hope go, and she slept peacefully.
story.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.

story.title: Action with devotion: surrender
story.summary: Krishna urges Arjuna to offer all action, warns that ego will only trip him, tells him to reflect fully and then choose, and finally to take refuge in him alone and not grieve.
story.lesson: Reflect fully, choose freely, and set down the fear.

days.reading: After eighteen chapters, the Lord tells Arjuna, 'Reflect on this fully, then do as you wish' (18.63). Because you are curious about where to begin, this shows that wisdom is offered freely, yet the final step remains yours. After that, he adds his last word: come to him alone for refuge, and do not grieve. You can hold that last word as you look at those Rishikesh hotels tonight.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You asked to hear a joke. Krishna tells Arjuna that people turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom, and all four kinds are welcome. Your curiosity itself places you among those who seek, so you can simply sit with this verse today as a starting point for your week with the Gita.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He explains that four kinds of people come to him. These are the ones in pain, the ones who want to know, the ones who need something, and the ones who already understand. He says all of them are good people and all of them worship him. Your curiosity places you among those who seek, right where this verse begins.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You asked about tomorrow's weather. Krishna tells Arjuna that people turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom, and all four are welcome. Your curiosity itself places you among those who seek, so let this verse meet you where you are right now, as you wonder what tomorrow brings.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He explains why most people miss the divine and who instead turns toward it. He names four kinds of good people who worship him. These are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He makes clear that every motive for turning toward the divine is welcome. Your curiosity about tomorrow fits exactly among those who turn toward something larger, without any need to justify the reason.

verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of people turn to the divine: those in distress, those seeking wealth, those seeking knowledge, and the wise. Your curiosity about who made this app places you in the company of the seeker of knowledge. That questioning mind is already a form of turning toward something larger.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He explains why most people miss the divine. Most are caught in the play of qualities. Yet four kinds of good people turn toward the divine. They come in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome. Your curiosity about who made this app places you among the seekers of knowledge. That questioning mind is already a form of turning toward something larger.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: My heart feels heavy as stone, but I don't cry, because of what people would think.
verse_text.translation: Though my heart is packed tight with the stones of life's sorrows, I don't let my tears fall, only out of fear of what my own people would think.

verse_text.speaker: Angiras
verse_text.setting: The two birds, continued.
verse_text.line: The bird that eats grieves, lost in its helplessness. When it sees the calm one beside it, grief falls away.
verse_text.translation: On the same tree a person sits sunk, grieving, bewildered by his own helplessness. When he sees the other, the content lord, and his greatness, his sorrow leaves him.

verse_text.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, CIII, p. 160
verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: Letter from Belur, 18 May 1901, ill and grieving the sudden death of the Raja of Khetri.
verse_text.line: Yet I am sure to bob up soon and am waiting for the next turn.
verse_text.translation: The Raja of Khetri died from a fall a few months ago. So you see things are all gloomy with me just now, and my own health is wretched. Yet I am sure to bob up soon and am waiting for the next turn.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: Closing verse of the section on steadfastness.
verse_text.line: A cut tree grows back; the waning moon fills again. Remembering this, the wise do not despair.
verse_text.translation: A tree that is cut grows again; the waning moon waxes again in the world. Reflecting on this, the good are not tormented in this world.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha on the fourth gatekeeper: good company (satsanga).
verse_text.line: Even at your lowest and most helpless, don't let go of good company.
verse_text.translation: Even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little.

verse_text.speaker: Kabandha
verse_text.setting: Ram is lost and grieving; Kabandha tells him to seek Sugriva, who has also lost his wife and home.
verse_text.line: Find a friend who knows your kind of trouble. You won't get through this alone.
verse_text.translation: You must make him your friend, best of friends. Thinking it over, I see no success for you without it.

story.title: Kabandha: find a friend who understands
story.summary: Freed from a curse, the creature Kabandha tells the grieving brothers to seek out Sugriva, an exile who has also lost his wife and home. Only a friend in the same trouble, he says, can help them now.
story.lesson: When you are lost, look for someone who has been through the same thing.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse_text.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse_text.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.

reading: Your body is reacting to real danger right now. Krishna hears Arjuna say, 'My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.' That panic is a true signal, not a failure. Let this trembling remind you that your own body is telling the truth about what is happening today.
meaning: Arjuna speaks these words to Krishna on the battlefield. He sees his own kin standing in the enemy ranks. His body collapses under the weight of grief and fear. He tells Krishna that his limbs fail him, his mouth goes dry, his body shakes, and his hair stands on end. The verse proposes that even a mighty warrior can freeze when faced with unbearable loss. It opens the teaching from a place of breakdown rather than bravery. Your body is reacting to real danger right now. That panic is a true signal, not a failure.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna's final counsel: act with devotion, reflect, choose, and take refuge.
verse_text.line: Lean on me alone. I will free you from every wrong. Don't worry.
verse_text.translation: Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone. I will free you from all sins; do not grieve.

reading: You feel uneasy while raising your kids. Krishna tells Arjuna, 'Abandon all dharmas and take refuge in me alone; I will free you from all sins, do not grieve.' This speaks to your today by saying you can lean on the divine alone when someone corners you and threatens disbelief. Let that refuge be the concrete place you stand in.
meaning: Krishna speaks these words to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between two armies and tells Krishna he is confused and afraid. Krishna has been guiding him through duty and action. Now Krishna urges him to set down every other support and take refuge in him alone. He promises to free Arjuna from all wrong and tells him not to grieve. When someone corners you and threatens disbelief, you can set down the burden of proving yourself and take refuge in the divine alone.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Narada asks why Ram stopped his marriage; Ram explains how he guards those who rely on him.
verse_text.line: Those who rely on me, I guard always, as a mother pulls her child back from the fire.
verse_text.translation: 'When I wanted to marry, Lord, why did you not let me?' 'Listen, sage, I tell you gladly: those who worship me, giving up every other reliance, I always guard, as a mother guards her child. When the little child runs to grab fire or a snake, the mother pulls it back.'

reading: You are living with a father who drinks and strikes your mother and you. Ram tells Narada that he always guards those who rely on him, pulling a child back from fire or a snake just as a mother does. In your home today, that fierce protection means you are not alone in the danger you face.
